PROBLEM

The kernel's TMA coordinates are ordered (row, col), but the shared descriptor helper `make_2d_tensor_map` (code/core/common/headers/tma_helpers.cuh:102-106) builds the CUtensorMap with dims={height,width} while cuTensorMapEncodeTiled defines globalDim[0] as the innermost/contiguous dimension and globalStrides[0] as the stride of dimension 1. With B stored row-major [K,N] (ld=N), the encoded map's address function is addr(c0,c1)=base+c0*4+c1*N*4, i.e. c0 is physically the COLUMN index. The kernel passes coords={k_base, tile_n*TILE_N}, so each 128x128 TMA fetch lands B_smem[kk][nn]=B[n_base+kk][k_base+nn] instead of the intended B[k_base+kk][n_base+nn] — a transposed, origin-swapped tile. The multicast GEMM therefore computes C=A·(permuted-Bᵀ): wrong math, and its VERIFY checksum can never match tma_multicast_baseline (whose manual smem loads at tma_multicast_baseline.cu:98 are correct), so the baseline-vs-multicast comparison this series' commits (775b05b16 'Fix SM103 TMA multicast build', f7ec105e0 'Fix TMA multicast shared memory builds') built verify binaries for is broken. The bug also propagates into the new hand-written SM103a PTX path (lines 91-102), which hardcodes the same operand order. It runs cleanly for the square 2048³ default (encode succeeds, all accesses in-bounds), so nothing fails visibly — and per HANDOFF.md ('Latest non-B200 checkpoint') the series was only ever compile-validated in a GPU-less container, never executed. The repo itself contains the correct convention: optimized_flash_attn_tma_micro_pipeline.cu:53-60 defines its own `make_2d_tensor_map_col_row` with dims={width,height}, stride={ld*4}, matching the NVIDIA driver contract, precisely because the shared helper is flipped.

EVIDENCE
tma_multicast_cluster.cu:167-168: `// Coordinates follow the descriptor's dimension order (row, col).` / `const int coords[2] = {k_base, tile_n * TILE_N};` — fed to both `cptx::cp_async_bulk_tensor(...)` (line 178) and the new `issue_tma_multicast_sm103(...)` asm (`"[%0], [%1, {%2, %3}], [%4], %5;"`, lines 91-102). Root cause in tma_helpers.cuh:102-106: `// Tensor map layout is {rows, cols}. We accept width/height inputs in the usual (cols, rows) order and flip them to match the driver API contract.` / `std::uint64_t dims[rank] = {static_cast<std::uint64_t>(height), static_cast<std::uint64_t>(width)};` with `stride[rank-1] = {ld * sizeof(float)}` — contradicted by the driver contract and by the repo's own correct variant, optimized_flash_attn_tma_micro_pipeline.cu:54-57: `std::uint64_t dims[rank] = { static_cast<std::uint64_t>(width), static_cast<std::uint64_t>(height) };`. Kernel consumption at tma_multicast_cluster.cu:207 expects `B_smem[kk][thread_n + j]` = B[k_base+kk][n_base+...].

SUGGESTED FIX

Fix `make_2d_tensor_map` in code/core/common/headers/tma_helpers.cuh to follow the driver contract like the `_col_row` variant: dims={width,height}, box={box_width,box_height} (delete the flip and its comment). In tma_multicast_cluster.cu change the coords to x-then-y: `const int coords[2] = {tile_n * TILE_N, k_base};` (same array feeds both the CCCL wrapper and the SM103a asm path) and correct the '(row, col)' comment. Then audit the helper's other callers (ch07/optimized_tma_bulk_tensor_2d.cu, ch07/optimized_tma_copy.cu, ch07/async_prefetch_2d_demo.cu, core/common/headers/cuda13_demos.cuh) for the same swap, and run tma_multicast_baseline_verify vs tma_multicast_cluster_verify on a B200 to confirm the checksums now agree.

VERIFIER NOTES

All quoted evidence exists verbatim. tma_helpers.cuh:104-107 encodes dims={height,width} with stride[0]=ld*4; per the cuTensorMapEncodeTiled contract (globalDim[0] = innermost/contiguous dim, globalStrides[0] = byte stride of dim 1 — the CUDA guide's row-major example is size={WIDTH,HEIGHT}, stride={WIDTH*elem}), the resulting address function is addr(c0,c1)=base+c0*4+c1*ld*4, i.e. c0 is physically the COLUMN. The helper's line-102 comment asserting the opposite is wrong. With the call site's width=N, height=K, ld=N (tma_multicast_cluster.cu:371-380) and kernel coords={k_base, tile_n*TILE_N} (line 168), each 128x128 fetch lands B_smem[kk][nn]=B[n_base+kk][k_base+nn] instead of B[k_base+kk][n_base+nn] consumed at line 207 — a transposed, origin-swapped tile. The same coords array feeds both the CCCL wrapper (line 178) and the SM103a asm path (lines 91-102), so both are wrong. Nothing compensates: tma_multicast_baseline.cu:93-98 loads B correctly by hand, so the two VERIFY checksums diverge for random inputs. The repo's own make_2d_tensor_map_col_row (optimized_flash_attn_tma_micro_pipeline.cu:43-58) uses the correct dims={width,height} convention, corroborating the flip. The square 2048^3 default runs cleanly (symmetric dims and box, all accesses in-bounds), and per HANDOFF the series was only compile-validated, so the bug is silent. Severity high stands: the baseline-vs-multicast verification this commit series built is broken, and the flipped helper has additional callers (ch07/optimized_tma_copy.cu, ch07/optimized_tma_bulk_tensor_2d.cu, ch07/async_prefetch_2d_demo.cu, core/common/headers/cuda13_demos.cuh, ch10/tma_2d_pipeline_blackwell.cu) that need the same audit.

sections:
PROBLEM

In the 4-stage mainloop, iteration k issues issue_tma(next_s, next_k) with next_s = (k+3)%4 == (k-1)%4, i.e. into the exact stage whose MMA was issued in the previous iteration. tcgen05.mma is asynchronous: the gemm() calls return immediately and the tensor core reads smem_A/smem_B until tcgen05.commit signals the empty barrier via umma_arrive. The code arrives on empty_barrier[curr] (lines 230-231) but NEVER calls wait_barrier on any empty_barrier before re-issuing TMA into that stage, so the cp.async.bulk write can land while the MMA is still reading, silently corrupting the accumulator. This is the lab's incumbent kernel (autotune.py maps "cluster" to matmul_tcgen05_cluster; optimized_tcgen05_matmul.py uses it; bench_dual_cta.py labels it "cluster (incumbent)"), and run_lab.py only validates under --verify. The same never-waited empty_barrier pattern is in tcgen05_no_wait.cu (line 236), tcgen05_no_wait_swizzle.cu, tcgen05_warp_parallel.cu, and experimental/tcgen05_tma_multicast.cu (line 242). The repo's own tcgen05_dual_cta.cu:294 shows the required wait_barrier(storage.empty_barrier[next_s], ...) before reuse.

SUGGESTED FIX

Before issue_tma(next_s, next_k), when next_k >= kStages, add cute::wait_barrier(storage.empty_barrier[next_s], empty_phase[next_s]); empty_phase[next_s] ^= 1; (tracking a per-stage empty phase array), exactly as tcgen05_dual_cta.cu lines 290-295 does. Apply the same fix to tcgen05_no_wait.cu, tcgen05_no_wait_swizzle.cu, tcgen05_warp_parallel.cu, and experimental/tcgen05_tma_multicast.cu.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: in iteration k, line 211 issue_tma(next_s=(k+3)%4=(k-1)%4) refills the stage whose MMA was issued in iteration k-1; the only wait in the loop is on full_barrier[curr] (line 215), and grep confirms no wait_barrier(empty_barrier[...]) anywhere in the file — lines 230-231 arrive on it but nothing consumes the phase. tcgen05.mma is async (the file's own mma_barrier/umma_arrive epilogue sync proves the code knows this), so the WAR hazard is real. tcgen05_dual_cta.cu:293-295 implements exactly the missing wait. Pattern reproduced in tcgen05_no_wait.cu (lines 231-236, whose comment admits 'we just trust the pipeline depth and issue unconditionally'), tcgen05_no_wait_swizzle.cu, tcgen05_warp_parallel.cu, and experimental/tcgen05_tma_multicast.cu (lines 241-243). Consumer claims also verified: autotune.py:96 maps 'cluster' to this kernel, optimized_tcgen05_matmul.py defaults to it, bench_dual_cta.py:123 labels it 'cluster (incumbent)'. Critical is fair: silent nondeterministic corruption in the lab's flagship kernel; the race is timing-dependent (TMA fetch latency usually exceeds one k-tile of MMA), which is why validation passes today.

PROBLEM

_capture_decode_graph captures one decode step whose KVCache.insert_kv uses host Python ints for the cache slot: 't0, t1 = self.pos, self.pos + T_add; self.kv_cache[layer_idx, 0, :, :, t0:t1] = k' (lines 277-280) and attends over a fixed-length view kv_cache[..., :t1]. Those offsets are baked into the captured kernels. _graph_decode then replays the graph on every subsequent step (line 584), only re-capturing when ids shape/device, mask presence, or cache_gen (which changes only when the cache storage GROWS, line 160) change. self.pos never advances during replay (no Python runs), so every decode step after the first rewrites the SAME cache slot P and attends over the same fixed prefix :P+1. In Engine.generate() (line 1069 path, no token_mask), any run with model.config.use_cuda_graphs=True (e.g. tests/test_engine_smoke.py line 33, benchmark_incremental_optimizations.py '+ use_cuda_graphs' config) silently generates garbage from the second generated token onward, while the benchmark reports it as a speedup.

EVIDENCE
cache_gen = getattr(kv_cache, "cache_gen", None)
        if (not self._graph_shapes_match(ids, attention_mask, token_mask)) or (cache_gen != self._graph_cache_gen):
            self._capture_decode_graph(ids, kv_cache, attention_mask, token_mask)
        self._graph_static_ids.copy_(ids)
        ...
        self._decode_graph.replay()
        return self._graph_output

SUGGESTED FIX

Make the KV write position a device-side tensor that the captured graph reads and increments on-GPU (index_copy_ with a position tensor, incremented by a captured kernel), and make the attention length static (attend over the full preallocated cache with a mask driven by the position tensor). Alternatively, re-capture per position or disable the graph path entirely until the cache is graph-safe; the current cache_gen/shape check is insufficient and must not gate replay correctness.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: insert_kv's no-token_mask path (lines 277-282) writes kv_cache[layer,0,:,:,t0:t1] using host ints from self.pos, and returns a fixed :t1 view — both baked into the captured graph. _graph_decode (575-585) re-captures only on shape/device/mask-presence or cache_gen change; cache_gen increments only in _maybe_grow_cache (line 160), and generate() preallocates the decode cache to prompt+max_tokens (line 1033-1034) so it never grows. _decode_graph_disabled is initialized False (366) and never set True anywhere (grep), so nothing rescues the path. self.pos advances only in Python, which does not run during replay — every step after the first rewrites slot P and attends over :P+1. generate() calls _execute_decode(ids, kv_cache_decode) with no token_mask (line 1069) and (B,1) CUDA ids, satisfying the graph gate (588-594). One nit: the parenthetical citing benchmark_incremental_optimizations.py is wrong — that script never builds an Engine (see finding on line 159) — but tests/test_engine_smoke.py line 33 does set use_cuda_graphs=True, and any GPU Engine run with the flag hits the bug. Critical is correct.

sections:
PROBLEM

The script constructs ZeroRedundancyOptimizer with overlap_with_ddp=True but registers a plain custom comm hook (line 140: ddp_model.register_comm_hook(state=dist.group.WORLD, hook=_reduce_scatter_allgather_hook)) instead of a hook built with torch.distributed.algorithms.ddp_comm_hooks.ddp_zero_hook.hook_with_zero_step. With overlap_with_ddp=True, local-optimizer initialization is deferred until a zero-step hook drives it, and ZeroRedundancyOptimizer.step() (torch 2.8: 'if self._overlap_with_ddp: logger.warning(...); return None') is a warning-only no-op. So every optimizer.step() at line 189 does nothing: parameters are never updated, AdamW math never executes, and 'sharded optimizer states' never even exist. The benchmark then compares against baseline_zero2_multigpu.py, which pays for a full AdamW step every iteration, so the reported 'optimized ZeRO-2' speedup is largely the cost of silently skipping the optimizer, and print_memory_stats reports 'Optimizer states: 0.00 MB' — fake memory savings from an optimizer that was never created. The docstring claim 'overlap reduce-scatter gradients with sharded optimizer states' is false: nothing is sharded and nothing overlaps with an optimizer step.

EVIDENCE
optimizer = ZeroRedundancyOptimizer(
            ddp_model.parameters(),
            overlap_with_ddp=True,
            parameters_as_bucket_view=True,
            **_optimizer_cfg(ddp_model.parameters(), args.learning_rate),
        )
...
            optimizer.step()   # line 189 — no-op when overlap_with_ddp=True

SUGGESTED FIX

setup.sh single-sources the torch pin from requirements_latest.txt (line 1809: PYTORCH_TORCH_VERSION="${REQ_TORCH_VERSION}" -> 2.9.1+cu130, a stable release), but the install step resolves against PYTORCH_CU130_INDEX, which is hardcoded to the NIGHTLY channel (line 372). Verified live: https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cu130/torch/ contains no torch-2.9.1* wheel (only 2.10.0.dev*), while the wheel exists on the stable index https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130/torch/. The PyPI extra-index cannot satisfy a +cu130 local-version pin, and the cached-wheel fallback is impossible because line 1785 deletes cached torch manylinux wheels ('find "${PYTORCH_WHEEL_DIR}" ... -name "torch-*-manylinux*.whl" -delete'). pip therefore fails and the script hits 'exit 1' at line 1930 on every clean run — the repo's canonical environment bootstrap cannot complete anywhere. The same broken index pair is reused for the TE-rebuild reinstall at lines 3708-3716. The stale header ('Installing PyTorch nightly 2.10 cu130 stack', line 1916) and code/README.md:138 ('PyTorch 2.10-dev') contradict the actual 2.9.1 pin.

EVIDENCE
Line 372: PYTORCH_CU130_INDEX_ROOT="https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cu130"  |  Line 1924: --index-url "${PYTORCH_CU130_INDEX}" \  |  requirements_latest.txt:104: torch==2.9.1+cu130

SUGGESTED FIX

Point PYTORCH_CU130_INDEX_ROOT at https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130 and PYTORCH_TORCH_FIND_LINKS at https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130/torch/ (or select nightly vs stable by whether the resolved pin contains '.dev'), for both install sites (lines 1923-1931 and 3708-3716); update the banner text and README's '2.10-dev' claim to the pinned 2.9.1+cu130 stack.

VERIFIER NOTES

All evidence verified: line 372 hardcodes PYTORCH_CU130_INDEX_ROOT to the nightly channel, line 374 points find-links at nightly/cu130/torch/, and lines 1803-1810 single-source PYTORCH_TORCH_VERSION from requirements_latest.txt:104 (torch==2.9.1+cu130, stable). Live check today: the nightly cu130 index carries only torch-2.14.0.dev* wheels (no 2.9.x at all), while the stable index https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130/torch/ has torch-2.9.1+cu130. PyPI as extra-index cannot satisfy a +cu130 local-version pin (PEP 440 requires exact local match). Line 1785 deletes cached torch manylinux wheels, and neither pip_cmd (line 474) nor the install command adds third_party/wheels as find-links, so there is no fallback; the install at 1923-1928 fails and line 1930 exits 1. The TE-rebuild reinstall at 3708-3716 reuses the same broken index pair. The stale banner (line 1915) and README 'PyTorch 2.10-dev' claim also check out. Canonical bootstrap cannot complete on a clean run; critical is fair.

The only workflow that invokes pytest enumerates a fixed allowlist of 28 test files (plus 3 cherry-picked node ids from test_validate_benchmark_pairs_tools.py, out of that file's 14 tests). code/tests contains 258 top-level + 9 integration test files; neither tier1-nightly.yml nor dual-arch-compare.yml runs pytest at all, and 'make test' (which runs tests/) is not called by any workflow. The suites the book's credibility rests on — test_anti_cheat_protections.py, test_anti_cheat_edge_cases.py, test_protection_effectiveness.py, test_verification.py, test_verification_e2e.py, test_expectations_integrity.py, the 25k-line test_benchmark_hygiene_regressions.py — are gated by nothing: a regression in any of them merges green. The enforcement-relevant tests in test_validate_benchmark_pairs_tools.py that CI skips include the CPU-runnable test_validate_all_pairs_timeout_kills_isolated_pair_descendants.

'b200: ARCH=sm_100' is a GNU make target-specific variable, but ../core/common/cuda_arch.mk computes CUDA_ARCH_GENCODE, ARCH_SUFFIX and CUDA_NVCC_ARCH_FLAGS with ':=' at parse time (cuda_arch.mk lines 78-107), before any target-specific value exists. Reproduced with a minimal makefile: the recipe echoes the alias's ARCH while the flags keep the parse-time arch. Concretely, on a B200 host 'make gb300' auto-detects sm_100, compiles -gencode arch=compute_100a into *_sm100 binaries, yet prints 'Building Chapter 1 examples with sm_103' — a silently wrong-arch build with a misleading log. On a GPU-less host the aliases die in cuda_arch.mk's parse-time auto-detect $(error) even though the user explicitly named the architecture. The same broken alias pattern exists in every chapter Makefile (ch01-ch20) and in labs/nvfp4_gemm and labs/ozaki_scheme.

EVIDENCE
ch01/Makefile:41-42: 'b200: ARCH=sm_100' / 'b200: clean all'  with cuda_arch.mk:87: 'CUDA_ARCH_GENCODE := -gencode arch=compute_100a,code=[sm_100a,compute_100a]'

SUGGESTED FIX

Turn the aliases into recursive invocations that pass ARCH on the command line so cuda_arch.mk re-evaluates, e.g. 'b200: ; $(MAKE) ARCH=sm_100 clean all' (likewise gb10/b300/gb300) in every chapter and lab Makefile — the same mechanism the working 'compare' target already uses.

VERIFIER NOTES

Reproduced with a minimal makefile: the recipe echoes the target-specific ARCH (sm_103) while flags keep the parse-time gencode (compute_100a), because cuda_arch.mk assigns CUDA_ARCH_GENCODE/CUDA_NVCC_ARCH_FLAGS with ':=' (lines 87, 107) during parsing, before target-specific 'b200: ARCH=sm_100' (ch01/Makefile:41) can apply. Also reproduced on this GPU-less host: 'make -n b200' in ch01 dies at cuda_arch.mk:49 '$(error ... Unable to auto-detect GPU architecture)' at parse time even though the alias names the arch. TARGET_SUFFIX is likewise parse-time, so binaries keep the detected arch's suffix while 'all' prints the alias's ARCH — misleading log confirmed. Pattern verified in all of ch01-ch20 plus labs/nvfp4_gemm and labs/ozaki_scheme. The built binaries do match their suffix (they are not mislabeled), but the alias silently ignores the user's architecture choice — high is defensible for a documented cross-arch entry point.

PROBLEM

The 50 timed kernels are launched into a stream created with cudaStreamNonBlocking (line 64), but start/stop events are recorded on the legacy default stream with no synchronization of `stream` before the stop record. The legacy stream does not synchronize with non-blocking streams, so the stop event completes immediately after being enqueued and cudaEventElapsedTime returns roughly the host-side loop time (microseconds), not kernel execution time for 50 passes over 33M elements. The paired optimized_thresholdtma.cu launches on stream 0 (`launch_threshold_tma_pipeline(..., 0)` at its line 86) with default-stream events, so it measures real GPU time. The published baseline-vs-TMA comparison is therefore inverted: the naive baseline reports a near-zero "Average kernel time" and the TMA version looks slower.

SUGGESTED FIX

Record both events on the stream doing the work: cudaEventRecord(start, stream) and cudaEventRecord(stop, stream), then cudaEventSynchronize(stop) before cudaEventElapsedTime. Alternatively launch on stream 0 like the optimized pair.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: line 64 creates the stream with cudaStreamNonBlocking, lines 74/79 record start/stop with no stream argument (legacy NULL stream), and threshold_common.cuh line 140 launches threshold_naive_kernel on the passed stream. Non-blocking streams are exempt from legacy-stream implicit synchronization, so stop completes without waiting for the 50 kernels; elapsed time is host enqueue time. Cross-checked optimized_thresholdtma.cu: lines 76/86 pass stream 0 and lines 82/89 record default-stream events, so the optimized side measures real GPU time. The baseline-vs-TMA comparison is genuinely inverted. High severity is correct.
findings.title: Baseline timing measures only host enqueue: events on legacy stream, kernels on non-blocking stream

PROBLEM

In the double-buffered cp.async loop, the wait before consuming tile T must leave at most (tiles_enqueued - T - 1) groups pending. The code uses `(tiles_enqueued - tiles_processed) > 0` to choose cp.async.wait_group 1 vs 0. On the final tile of a block (tiles_processed = tiles_for_block - 1, tiles_enqueued = tiles_for_block), the difference is 1, so wait_group 1 is executed — which permits the one still-pending group (the copy for the very tile about to be consumed) to remain in flight. The subsequent reads of tile_ptr[i] can observe stale data from the previous tile that occupied that stage (or uninitialized smem for tiles_for_block==2, where the tile-1 group has never been waited on at all). Every block with tiles_for_block >= 2 races on its final tile; this is the ch08 'optimized' threshold path (launch_threshold_predicated_async), so it can nondeterministically produce wrong output values.

SUGGESTED FIX

Change the condition to `const bool keep_inflight = (tiles_enqueued - tiles_processed) > 1;` so that when only the about-to-be-consumed group is outstanding, cp.async.wait_group 0 is issued (all groups drained) before reading the stage buffer.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified by tracing. cp.async.wait_group N waits for all but the N most recent groups. For T=tiles_for_block=4: at end of iteration p=2, tiles_enqueued=4, tiles_processed=3, so keep_inflight=(4-3)>0 → wait_group 1 (lines 133-134), which permits the most recent group — the copy for tile 3, the very tile consumed next iteration — to remain in flight; iteration p=3 then reads stage buffer that may hold tile 1's stale data. Same for T=3; for T=2 the group for tile 1 is never drained at all before consumption (prologue and loop both issue wait_group 1). Only T=1 is safe (wait_group 0). The proposed fix ('> 1') is correct: when exactly one group is outstanding it is the about-to-be-consumed one and must be drained. Genuine data race on the final tile of every block with >=2 tiles in the ch08 optimized path; nondeterministic wrong output. High is appropriate.

The block-to-tile swizzle assumes every N-group has GROUP_SIZE=8 columns. When grid_n % 8 != 0 (any n where (n/256) % 8 != 0, e.g. m=256, n=512: grid_m=2, grid_n=2), the linear->tile map is not a bijection: the wrap `tile_n = tile_n % grid_n` makes multiple blocks compute the same tile while other (tile_m, tile_n) pairs are never assigned. For m=256/n=512 all four blocks get tile_m=0, so tiles with tile_m=1 are never computed. The output d_buffer is created with torch::empty (uninitialized), so the unwritten 128-row bands come back as garbage. The TORCH_CHECK at line 277 only requires m%128==0 && n%256==0 && k%64==0, so these broken shapes are accepted and the function silently returns wrong data.

SUGGESTED FIX

Use a partial-group-aware rasterization: int first_n = (linear_idx / (GROUP_SIZE * grid_m)) * GROUP_SIZE; int group_width = min(GROUP_SIZE, grid_n - first_n); int local = linear_idx - first_n * grid_m; tile_m = local / group_width; tile_n = first_n + local % group_width; (the standard CUTLASS threadblock-swizzle handling). Alternatively tighten the TORCH_CHECK to also require (n/256) % 8 == 0.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified. Lines 75-84: grid has exactly grid_m*grid_n blocks, but the swizzle assumes full 8-column groups; the wrap 'tile_n %= grid_n' makes the map non-bijective for grid_n%8!=0. Traced the reviewer's example (m=256,n=512 → grid_m=2,grid_n=2, 4 blocks): all four get tile_m=0 and tile_n wraps to {0,1,0,1}, so tiles (1,0),(1,1) are never computed while (0,0),(0,1) are computed twice. d_buffer is torch::empty (line 281, uninitialized) and TORCH_CHECK (line 277) only requires m%128/n%256/k%64, so such shapes are accepted and return garbage rows. Mitigating context: the repo's own benchmark (optimized_tcgen05_warp_specialization.py) uses 16384x16384 (grid_n=64, multiple of 8), so shipped benchmarks are unaffected — but the exported torch op silently corrupts many accepted shapes (any grid_n not a multiple of 8, e.g. n=512, 768, 1792, 2304). High is appropriate.

PROBLEM

The 'Timed iteration' records start/stop on the legacy default stream (cudaEventRecord(start) / cudaEventRecord(stop) with no stream argument) but launches all compute_kernel work into compute_streams[i], each created with cudaStreamCreateWithFlags(..., cudaStreamNonBlocking) (line 67). Non-blocking streams have NO implicit synchronization with the legacy default stream, so the stop event completes without waiting for any kernel. The printed "Kernel time: %.4f ms" is just the CPU enqueue time of the launch loop (microseconds), not kernel execution time — and parse_kernel_time_ms() in the harness picks up exactly this bogus number as the benchmark result.

EVIDENCE
CUDA_CHECK(cudaEventRecord(start));  ... compute_kernel<<<local_grid, block, 0, compute_streams[i]>>>(...) x3 ...  CUDA_CHECK(cudaEventRecord(stop));  CUDA_CHECK(cudaEventSynchronize(stop));  (lines 118-128), with CUDA_CHECK(cudaStreamCreateWithFlags(&compute_streams[i], cudaStreamNonBlocking)); at line 67.

SUGGESTED FIX

After the launch loop and before cudaEventRecord(stop), make the default stream wait on each compute stream (cudaEventRecord on each compute stream + cudaStreamWaitEvent on stream 0), or simply cudaDeviceSynchronize() then use CPU timing; alternatively record stop on each compute stream and take the max elapsed.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: cudaEventRecord(start)/(stop) with no stream argument (lines 118, 127) target the legacy NULL stream; all compute_kernel launches go to compute_streams[i] created with cudaStreamNonBlocking (line 67). Per CUDA semantics, non-blocking streams have no implicit synchronization with the legacy default stream, so the stop event completes without waiting for any kernel; prior work was fully synced at lines 105-110, so elapsed_ms is just host enqueue time for 9 launches. The printed 'Kernel time' (line 132) is bogus by orders of magnitude. One caveat: the finding's harness-parsing claim is contingent — this demo's wrapper (streams_ordered_demo.py via run_cuda_demo) only builds and runs the binary; parse_kernel_time_ms applies to CudaBinaryBenchmark-wrapped binaries. The invalid measurement itself is unambiguous.

PROBLEM

For each chunk i, memory is allocated stream-ordered on compute_streams[i] (lines 79-80), the H2D copy runs on h2d_streams[i] (line 82), the three compute kernels run on compute_streams[i] (lines 90-93), and the D2H copy runs on d2h_streams[i] (line 101) - with zero cudaEventRecord/cudaStreamWaitEvent calls anywhere in the file. All three per-chunk stream sets execute concurrently: the compute kernels can read d_in[i] before the H2D copy has written it, the D2H copy can read d_in[i] while kernels are still writing it, and per the stream-ordered allocator contract, touching cudaMallocAsync memory from a stream not ordered after the allocation is undefined behavior. The demo produces nondeterministic h_src results and teaches broken multi-stream pipelining.

SUGGESTED FIX

Bridge the stages with events: record an event on h2d_streams[i] after the cudaMemcpyAsync and cudaStreamWaitEvent it on compute_streams[i]; record an event after the last compute kernel and wait on it in d2h_streams[i]. Also make the allocation visible to h2d_streams[i] (allocate on h2d_streams[i], or record an event after cudaMallocAsync on compute_streams[i] and wait on it in h2d_streams[i]).

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: allocation on compute_streams[i] (lines 79-80), H2D on h2d_streams[i] (line 82), kernels on compute_streams[i] (lines 90-93), D2H on d2h_streams[i] (lines 101-102), all nine streams cudaStreamNonBlocking (lines 66-68). Grep confirms zero cudaStreamWaitEvent calls in the file; the only cudaEventRecord calls (118/127) are timing, placed after the enqueues, and the stream syncs at 105-110 come after everything is already racing. Kernels can read d_in before the copy lands, D2H can read mid-compute, and using cudaMallocAsync memory from unordered streams violates the stream-ordered allocator contract. High is fair: nondeterministic output and a teaching demo of exactly the wrong pattern.

The 'Original kernel' timed loop executes TWO scale_kernel launches per iteration (scale by 1.1f then 1.05f, lines 221-222), while the vectorized loop (line 257) and async loop (line 278) execute ONE kernel per iteration over the same N elements. The printed speedups at lines 395-401 (ms_original/ms_vectorized and ms_original/ms_async) therefore credit the optimized kernels with roughly half the work, inflating the claimed vectorization/async speedup by ~2x. The GB/s figures (2.0f*BYTES per iter) are also wrong for the baseline, which actually moves ~4x BYTES per iteration.

EVIDENCE
for (int i = 0; i < ITERS; ++i) { ... scale_kernel<<<grid, block, 0, stream1>>>(d_a, N, 1.1f); scale_kernel<<<grid, block, 0, stream1>>>(d_a, N, 1.05f); }  vs the vectorized loop's single scale_kernel_vectorized_float8<<<grid_vec, block, 0, stream1>>>(d_a, N, 1.1f); and printf("Vectorized kernel: ... [%.2fx speedup]", ..., ms_original / ms_vectorized) at lines 395-397.

SUGGESTED FIX

Launch the same number of kernels (one per iteration) in the baseline loop, or launch two vectorized kernels per iteration to match; recompute the GB/s figure from the actual per-iteration byte traffic of each variant.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: baseline timed loop (lines 219-223) launches scale_kernel twice per iteration (1.1f then 1.05f); vectorized loop (lines 254-261) and async loop (lines 276-279) launch once per iteration over the same N. Printed speedups ms_original/ms_vectorized and ms_original/ms_async (lines 395-401) therefore credit the optimized kernels with half the work — ~2x inflation. GB/s claim also verified: all three variants use 2.0f*BYTES per iteration (lines 393-399), but the baseline actually moves ~4x BYTES per iteration (2 passes x read+write), so its GB/s is understated ~2x. Event timing here is correctly on stream1, so the numbers are real — just an apples-to-oranges comparison.

PROBLEM

The timed loop launches fused_bias_kernel pairs into streams created with cudaStreamCreateWithFlags(..., cudaStreamNonBlocking) (line 120), but start and stop are recorded on the legacy default stream and stop is recorded immediately after the launch loop with no cudaStreamSynchronize of the work streams first. Because the legacy stream does not synchronize with non-blocking streams, cudaEventSynchronize(stop) returns without waiting for any kernel, and the printed "Kernel time: %.4f ms" is only the host-side launch-loop duration - a bogus number for the multi-stream benchmark this demo represents.

SUGGESTED FIX

Synchronize all work streams before recording stop (for (auto& s : streams) CUDA_CHECK(cudaStreamSynchronize(s)); then cudaEventRecord(stop)), and record start after a cudaDeviceSynchronize so the interval brackets the GPU work; or time with events recorded per-stream and take the max elapsed.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: streams created cudaStreamNonBlocking at line 120; timed loop 186-195 records start/stop with no stream argument and records stop immediately after the launch loop with no cudaStreamSynchronize of the work streams first (the syncs at 176-179 precede the timed section). stop completes immediately on the empty legacy stream, so the printed "Kernel time" at line 200 is host enqueue time. Verification (lines 204-211) is unaffected since h_out came from the earlier, properly synced loop. Medium is right: the benchmark number is bogus but results are not corrupted.
findings.title: Same wrong-stream event timing: stop event does not wait for kernels launched on non-blocking streams

PROBLEM

Both cudaEventRecord calls omit the stream argument (legacy default stream), while the 20 cudaGraphLaunch calls (each embedding 6000 kernels: CAPTURE_ITERS=1000 x 6 stages) go to `stream` created with cudaStreamNonBlocking (line 78). The stop event does not wait for the non-blocking stream, so the measured time is just the host time to enqueue 20 graph launches (~microseconds), excluding essentially all 120,000 kernel executions. baseline_cuda_graphs.cu has the identical bug at its lines 91/96, but its 120,000 individual launches hit launch-queue backpressure, so its measured host time approaches real GPU time. The printed baseline-vs-graph "ms/iter" comparison therefore exaggerates the CUDA-graphs speedup by orders of magnitude instead of showing the true launch-overhead saving. Note the sibling pair ch12/baseline_graph_bandwidth.cu / optimized_graph_bandwidth.cu does this correctly with cudaEventRecord(start, stream).

SUGGESTED FIX

In both optimized_cuda_graphs.cu (lines 107/112) and baseline_cuda_graphs.cu (lines 91/96), record the events on the work stream: cudaEventRecord(start, stream) / cudaEventRecord(stop, stream), then cudaEventSynchronize(stop) (or keep the stream sync) before cudaEventElapsedTime.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: line 78 creates the non-blocking stream; lines 107/112 record events with no stream argument while line 110 launches the graph into `stream`; line 113 syncs the stream only after stop is recorded, which does not help the event interval. baseline_cuda_graphs.cu has the identical pattern at lines 91/96 (work on non-blocking stream from line 71), but its 20000x6 = 120,000 individual launches saturate the launch queue so host time approaches GPU time, while 20 graph launches enqueue near-instantly. The printed speedup is therefore inflated far beyond the real launch-overhead saving. High severity is correct.
findings.title: Graph-replay benchmark records events on default stream while replays run on non-blocking stream

sections:
PROBLEM

Each thread accumulates only its own strided slice of the q.k dot product (`for (int d = threadIdx.x; d < head_dim; d += blockDim.x)`), then immediately exponentiates that per-thread partial (`half weight = hexp(score)`) with no cross-thread reduction (no __shfl/shared-memory sum, no barrier). With blockDim.x >= head_dim each thread's `score` is a single q[d]*k[d] product, so the kernel computes out[d] = sum_pos exp(q_d*k_pos,d) * v[pos,d] / sum_pos exp(q_d*k_pos,d) - an independent per-dimension 'softmax', not attention. There is also no running-max subtraction, so the fp16 hexp overflows to inf for any moderately large score. The Chapter 18 sample therefore teaches a decode kernel whose output bears no relation to scaled-dot-product attention; the 'sketch' disclaimer covers omitted error handling, not incorrect math.

SUGGESTED FIX

Reduce `score` across the block (warp shuffle + shared-memory reduction over head_dim) before the exp; keep a running max and accumulate acc/denom in fp32 (online softmax), then have each thread write its out[d] from the block-shared weight. Alternatively re-label and rewrite the sample as one-thread-per-(batch,head) so the loop over d is genuinely a full dot product.
findings.title: FlashMLA book sample computes softmax of per-thread partial dot products - the attention math is wrong

The root callback runs `from cli.tui import run_tui` when no subcommand is given (the documented default: "no args -> launch the benchmark TUI"). No `cli/tui.py` or `cli/tui/` package exists anywhere in the repo (and never has, per git history), so plain `aisp` raises ModuleNotFoundError with a raw traceback. The import sits OUTSIDE the try/except at lines 268-272, so the "TUI error" handler never fires. The same dead import is at line 2046 (`aisp tui` command). Only core/benchmark/bench_commands.py:4226 wraps the import in an ImportError fallback.

SUGGESTED FIX

Either restore/add the cli/tui module, or make both call sites degrade gracefully: move the import inside the try block and, on ImportError, print a message (or fall back to `core.benchmark.bench_commands._run_basic_menu` like bench_commands.py does) instead of crashing the documented default entrypoint.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: `@app.callback(invoke_without_command=True)` (line 250) runs the callback on bare `aisp`, and line 267 `from cli.tui import run_tui` sits outside the try/except at 268-272. code/cli/ contains only __init__.py, aisp.py, commands/ — no tui module; executing `import cli.tui` with code/ on sys.path raises ModuleNotFoundError. Same dead import at aisp.py:2046; only bench_commands.py:4226 has an ImportError fallback. One nit: 'never has, per git history' is wrong — a tui.py historically existed at code/tools/cli/tui.py (commit f2646de5e), not code/cli/tui.py — but that doesn't change the defect. High stands: the documented default entrypoint crashes with a raw traceback.

measure_hbm_bandwidth times y.copy_(x), a device-to-device copy that reads size_bytes and writes size_bytes (2x size_bytes of HBM traffic per iteration), but the bandwidth formula counts only size_bytes. The reported 'peak_bandwidth_tbs' is therefore half the achieved memory traffic: a B200 copy running near its 8 TB/s HBM3e peak reports ~3.5-4 TB/s and 'peak_utilization_percent' ~45%. This halved number is then persisted as the baseline target used by performance_targets.py (whose default hbm3e target of 3.0-3.5 TB/s codifies the error), making every chapter's bandwidth-efficiency claims wrong by 2x. measure_l2_cache_bandwidth (line 611) has the identical error.

EVIDENCE
for _ in range(iterations): y.copy_(x)  ... bandwidth_gbs = (size_bytes * iterations / elapsed_s) / 1e9  (lines 191-200); comment at 203-204: '# Theoretical peak for B200 is ~8.0 TB/s'.

SUGGESTED FIX

Count read+write traffic: bandwidth_gbs = (2 * size_bytes * iterations / elapsed_s) / 1e9 in both measure_hbm_bandwidth and measure_l2_cache_bandwidth, and rebase the stored hbm3e/L2 targets accordingly.

TILE_M = TILE_N = 64 (lines 242-243) and dim3 block(TILE_N, TILE_M) = 4096 threads is passed to cudaLaunchKernelExC — every warmup and benchmark launch returns cudaErrorInvalidConfiguration, so the benchmark prints "Kernel launch failed" and returns 1; it has never produced a valid measurement. Independently, even with a legal block the kernel has a shared-memory race: in the main loop each thread calls barriers[stage].arrive() and then immediately overwrites smem_A/smem_B[stage] (lines 98-120) while other threads may still be reading that same stage in the compute loop (lines 88-96) — arrive() does not block, and the barrier wait comes only after the writes. Finally, the summary prints "TMEM: Tensor memory data path" and "Warp Spec: Pipelined execution" although the kernel contains no tcgen05/TMEM instructions and no warp specialization.

EVIDENCE
Lines 242-243: "const int TILE_M = 64;\n    const int TILE_N = 64;" and line 275: "dim3 block(TILE_N, TILE_M);" feeding config.blockDim for cudaLaunchKernelExC; feature banner at lines ~365-370 prints "✓ TMEM: Tensor memory data path".

SUGGESTED FIX

Reduce the block to <=1024 threads (e.g. 32x32 with TILE_M=TILE_N=32, or per-thread micro-tiles). Move the compute-vs-prefetch separation to a real two-phase barrier: wait for all readers (a __syncthreads() or the barrier wait) BEFORE any thread writes the stage being reused. Remove or implement the TMEM/warp-spec claims in the printed feature list.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: TILE_M=TILE_N=64 (lines 242-243), dim3 block(TILE_N, TILE_M) (line 275) feeds cudaLaunchKernelExC (lines 294, 311); every launch returns cudaErrorInvalidConfiguration, warmup ignores it, and the benchmark loop prints 'Kernel launch failed' and returns 1 (lines 316-319). The summary prints '✓ TMEM: Tensor memory data path' (line 363) and '✓ Warp Spec: Pipelined execution' (line 368) though the kernel contains no tcgen05/TMEM instruction and no warp specialization. TILE_M and TILE_N are both 64 (lines 230-231) and the block is dim3(TILE_N, TILE_M) = (64,64) = 4096 threads. CUDA's maximum is 1024 threads per block on every GPU including B200, so both tma_gemm_kernel and tma_pipelined_gemm_kernel fail at launch with cudaErrorInvalidConfiguration. The program then verifies uninitialized/zeroed d_C, prints "FAILED", and computes TFLOPS/GB/s from the elapsed time of launches that never ran. This test binary (built by the Makefile 'all' target and run by its 'run' target) can never pass on any hardware. Additionally the file contains no TMA at all — the kernels are ordinary __shared__ loads with __syncthreads — yet reports "Basic TMA: %.2f TFLOPS".

EVIDENCE
Lines 230-231: "const int TILE_M = 64;\n    const int TILE_N = 64;" and line 255: "dim3 block1(TILE_N, TILE_M);" then line 263 launches "tma_gemm_kernel<TILE_M, TILE_N, TILE_K><<<grid1, block1>>>(d_A, d_B, d_C, M, N, K);".

SUGGESTED FIX

Use a legal block, e.g. TILE_M = TILE_N = 32 with dim3 block(32,32) (and grid scaled accordingly), or keep 64x64 tiles with a 2D thread block of at most 1024 threads and per-thread micro-tiles. Make the test exit nonzero on launch error instead of continuing to verification, and either implement real cp.async.bulk.tensor TMA or rename/relabel the test so it does not claim to measure TMA.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: TILE_M=TILE_N=64 (lines 230-231), dim3 block1(TILE_N, TILE_M) (line 255) = 4096 threads, launched at lines 263 and 287. maxThreadsPerBlock is 1024 on every CUDA GPU including SM 10.0, so both launches fail with cudaErrorInvalidConfiguration; the code prints the error but continues to verify never-written d_C (uninitialized for test 1, memset-0 for test 2), prints FAILED, and reports TFLOPS/GB/s from event timings of launches that never ran. The Makefile 'all' target builds it and 'run' executes it (lines 12, 17-18, 45). Also verified there is no TMA instruction in the file — both kernels are ordinary __shared__ + __syncthreads GEMMs (the comment at line 46 admits it) yet line 312 prints 'Basic TMA: %.2f TFLOPS'. High is fair for a shipped test that cannot pass on any hardware.

get_chapter_metric_config() maps chapter metrics named 'speedup', 'stream_speedup', 'fp8_speedup', etc. to the metric path 'timing.mean_ms' with MetricDirection.HIGHER_IS_BETTER. In compare_all_metrics(), line 826 does merged_config.update(chapter_config), which OVERWRITES the stock METRIC_CONFIG entry "timing.mean_ms": ("Mean Execution Time", LOWER_IS_BETTER, ...). For any chapter whose performance_targets define a speedup metric (ch10 stream_speedup, ch13, ch16 speedup/fp8_speedup, ch19 — and ch10 is the documented example in example_multi_metric_comparison.py line 67), every timing.mean_ms comparison is then evaluated as higher-is-better: an optimized run that is 2x SLOWER is reported as an improvement, and a 2x faster run is reported as a regression.

EVIDENCE
Line 578: "speedup": ("timing.mean_ms", "Speedup", MetricDirection.HIGHER_IS_BETTER, "x"),  ... Line 826: merged_config.update(chapter_config)  ... overwriting line 181: "timing.mean_ms": ("Mean Execution Time", MetricDirection.LOWER_IS_BETTER, "ms", 5.0, 5.0),

SUGGESTED FIX

Speedup is a derived metric, not an extractable path. Remove the timing.mean_ms mappings for all *speedup* chapter metrics (or map them to a distinct synthetic key like 'derived.speedup' computed as baseline_mean/optimized_mean), and make merged_config.update() refuse to change the direction of an existing METRIC_CONFIG entry.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: line 578-585 map speedup-named chapter metrics to path 'timing.mean_ms' with HIGHER_IS_BETTER; get_chapter_metric_config keys its dict by metric_path (line 656), and the guard at line 647 only checks the chapter-local dict, not METRIC_CONFIG. compare_all_metrics line 826 merged_config.update(chapter_config) overwrites METRIC_CONFIG line 181 (timing.mean_ms LOWER_IS_BETTER), and compare_metric (lines 769-780) then treats a larger mean time as an improvement. Detail correction: 'stream_speedup' is ch11, not ch10 (performance_targets.py line 115 is inside the ch11 block; ch10 has only tflops/utilization metrics, so the ch10 example at example_multi_metric_comparison.py:67 does not trigger the bug). Affected chapters are ch11, ch13 (compiled_autograd_speedup), ch14 (torch_compile_speedup_large), ch16 (speedup, fp8_speedup), ch19 (fp8_training_speedup). Core defect is real: timing regressions are inverted for those chapters.

The optimized async-input-pipeline path (used by labs/async_input_pipeline baseline+optimized) allocates each GPU batch inside `with torch.cuda.stream(self.copy_stream)` (line 110) and consumes it on the compute stream (benchmark_fn lines 164-176). No `record_stream()` is ever called (grep confirms the only record_stream calls in the repo are in core/harness and core/benchmark). When the Python refs to a batch are dropped (self._last_batch is overwritten each iteration, line 172), the caching allocator tags the block free for its allocation stream (copy_stream) only. Two iterations later `_launch_h2d` can reuse that exact block for the next H2D copy while the compute stream's model forward on the old batch is still in flight — the async H2D overwrites tensor memory being read, silently corrupting inputs and benchmark output. This is the canonical prefetcher bug that NVIDIA's reference prefetchers fix with `batch.record_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream())`, and it matches the repo's confirmed cross-stream reuse-buffer race class (moe_hybrid_ep, moe_cuda kv_transfer).

EVIDENCE
with torch.cuda.stream(self.copy_stream), self._nvtx_range(label):
            batch_gpu = batch_cpu.to(self.device, non_blocking=self.cfg.non_blocking)
            event.record(self.copy_stream)
... (benchmark_fn) self._last_batch = batch_gpu.detach()
            with torch.no_grad():
                out = self.model(batch_gpu)

SUGGESTED FIX

In benchmark_fn, after `self.compute_stream.wait_event(self._prefetch_event)`, call `batch_gpu.record_stream(self.compute_stream)` (and likewise record the compute stream on any tensor produced on the copy stream before its refs are dropped), or keep batches alive until a compute-stream event recorded after the forward pass has completed.

`llm_call` computes tokens as the MAX of the caller override, config value, and a hardcoded 131072 floor (and `from_env` line 62 does `env_max = max(env_max, 131072)`, so LLM_MAX_TOKENS/PERF_LLM_MAX_TOKENS can never lower it). The docstring says `max_tokens: Override default max_tokens`, and the config comment claims "cap to provider constraints at call time", but no cap exists anywhere. Result: every request sends max_tokens=131072. Anthropic rejects >64000 output tokens for the default claude-sonnet-4 model and OpenAI chat completions rejects >16384 for gpt-4o with a 400 invalid_request_error, so llm_call always fails on the default configurations. Additionally `get_llm_status(probe=True)` calls `llm_call("LLM connectivity check", max_tokens=64)` (line 413) — the 64 is silently discarded, so the connectivity probe reports the backend unavailable even with a valid key.

EVIDENCE
tokens = max(
        t for t in [
            max_tokens if max_tokens is not None else 0,
            config.max_tokens or 0,
            131072,
        ] if isinstance(t, (int, float))
    )

SUGGESTED FIX

Honor the override: `tokens = max_tokens if max_tokens is not None else config.max_tokens` and drop the 131072 floor in both llm_call and LLMConfig.from_env (line 62); if a floor is desired, clamp DOWN to per-provider/model output limits before sending (e.g. min(tokens, provider_max)).

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: lines 208-214 take max(override, config, 131072) so the floor always wins and overrides can only raise; from_env line 62 does `env_max = max(env_max, 131072)`. Grep confirms no min()/clamp anywhere in llm.py — max_tokens=131072 goes straight into _call_openai (max_tokens/max_output_tokens), _call_anthropic, etc. Anthropic rejects max_tokens above the 64000 output cap of default claude-sonnet-4-20250514 with a 400, and OpenAI chat completions rejects >16384 for default gpt-4o, so both default configs fail on every call. Probe at line 413 passes max_tokens=64 which line 210's max() discards, making get_llm_status(probe=True) report unavailable. High is correct.

Multiple docs state GB300 (Blackwell Ultra) per-GPU dense peaks of FP8 7.5 PFLOPS and BF16/FP16 3.75 PFLOPS. NVIDIA's Blackwell Ultra uplift applies only to dense NVFP4 (15 PFLOPS); FP8 stays at ~5 PFLOPS dense and FP16/BF16 at ~2.5 PFLOPS dense, unchanged from GB200's B200. The repo's own measurements prove it: code/docs/gb300-runbook.md:1659 records cuBLAS BF16 asymptoting at 1.87 PF at 8192^3 with a measured per-SM UMMA rate of ~64ns per 128x256x16 tile (16.4 TF/SM x 148 SMs = ~2.4 PF hardware ceiling) and recommends 'adopt ~1.9 PF as the GB300 dense-fp16 SoL reference (current sol-ceilings framing overstates remaining headroom 2x)'. Line 6 (set(CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES 100)) makes CMake add its own compute_100/sm_100 pass to every compile AND drive the CUDA_SEPARABLE_COMPILATION device-link step with that architecture only. The feature-specific 'a' targets that the CUTLASS SM100 tcgen05 kernel requires (cutlass_gemm.cu is guarded by '#if defined(CUTLASS_ARCH_MMA_SM100_SUPPORTED)' at line 29 with a TORCH_CHECK(false, "CUTLASS SM100 not supported - requires Blackwell GPU") fallback at line 167) are injected only as compile options (lines 50-51), which CMake's device-link step never sees. The sm_100a/sm_103a relocatable device code is therefore not in the linked device module; what survives is the plain compute_100 pass — so the build either fails at ptxas/device-link, or produces a .so whose kernel raises 'requires Blackwell GPU' at runtime even on an actual B200/B300. CUTLASS SM100 kernels are documented to require the arch-conditional 100a/103a targets, so the plain-100 pass added by line 6 is wrong in every case.

EVIDENCE
Line 6: set(CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES 100)  |  Lines 50-51: '-gencode=arch=compute_100a,code=sm_100a' / '-gencode=arch=compute_103a,code=sm_103a'  |  Line 66: CUDA_SEPARABLE_COMPILATION ON

SUGGESTED FIX

Delete the two manual -gencode lines and set the arch list once: set(CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES "100a;103a") (and pass -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=100a;103a in build.sh line 15 instead of 100), so compile and device-link use the same feature-enabled targets.

VERIFIER NOTES

Evidence verified at lines 6, 50-51, 66. CMake's device-link step for a CUDA_SEPARABLE_COMPILATION target is driven solely by the CUDA_ARCHITECTURES property (=100 from line 6); per-target compile options never reach nvcc -dlink, so the sm_100a/sm_103a relocatable device code is not device-linked — standard nvcc/CMake behavior, correctly described. One mechanism detail is wrong: I fetched cutlass arch/config.h at the pinned submodule commit (57e3cfb4) and CUTLASS_ARCH_MMA_SM100_SUPPORTED is toolkit-version-gated (nvcc >= 12.8), not arch-gated, so with the repo's CUDA 13 toolchain the '#else TORCH_CHECK(false, requires Blackwell GPU)' fallback at cutlass_gemm.cu:166-167 never compiles; the failure instead surfaces as a ptxas/device-link error on the plain compute_100 pass or a CUTLASS runtime failure from the crippled non-a sm_100 kernel (tcgen05 requires the arch-conditional 100a/103a targets, matching the finding's first alternative). Core defect real: the plain-100 arch driving compile+dlink is wrong in every case, and build.sh:15 passes -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=100 as claimed.

PROBLEM

The host rounds grid_m up to a multiple of the cluster size, but gemm_cluster uses tile_m = blockIdx.x directly with no check against the real number of M tiles. TORCH_CHECK only requires m % 128 == 0, so any m with an odd number of 128-row tiles (m = 128, 384, 1920, ...) creates a padded CTA whose epilogue executes plain global stores (copy(tDrAcc, tDgD)) of a 128x256 fp32 tile starting at row m — 128 KB written past the end of d_buffer, corrupting neighboring allocations in the CUDA caching allocator. (The A/B loads survive only because TMA clamps/zero-fills OOB coordinates; the epilogue stores are ordinary STG instructions with no such protection.) experimental/tcgen05_tma_multicast.cu line 345 has the identical bug.

EVIDENCE
Line 308-309: "// Grid must be divisible by cluster size\n  if (grid_m % 2 != 0) grid_m += 1;" while the kernel (line 79) does "int tile_m = blockIdx.x;  // Unique per CTA" with no bounds check, and the epilogue (line 251) does "copy(tDrAcc, tDgD);  // D = accumulator (beta=0)" unconditionally.

SUGGESTED FIX

Either require m % 256 == 0 in the TORCH_CHECK (so grid_m is always even), or add an early-out guard in the kernel: if (tile_m * 128 >= size<0>(shape(mA))) return; — placed before any cluster-wide barrier usage so both CTAs of a padded cluster exit together (with the multicast variant, guard before cluster_sync or make the whole padded cluster exit).

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: lines 308-309 pad grid_m to even; TORCH_CHECK (line 272) only requires m % 128 == 0, so m=128 already yields grid_m 1->2. The kernel uses tile_m = blockIdx.x (line 79) with no comparison against the real M-tile count, and the epilogue copy(tDrAcc, tDgD) at line 251 is unconditional plain stores — CuTe local_tile does pure offset arithmetic with no clamping, and d_buffer is torch::empty({m,n}) with no slack, so the padded CTA stores a 128x256 fp32 tile (128 KB) past the allocation per grid_n column. TMA loads for the padded tile are saved only by tensor-map OOB handling, as the finding says. experimental/tcgen05_tma_multicast.cu lines 344-345 plus its unconditional epilogue (line 286) has the identical bug. High is correct: heap corruption in the incumbent kernel for any odd number of M tiles.

PROBLEM

The host wrapper validates bias (length must equal n, converted to fp32) and passes bias_contig.data_ptr to the kernel with fuse_bias_silu=true, but the fused epilogue never reads bias_ptr: the code sets x = acc_val and applies SiLU only. Any caller (the function is exported via PYBIND11 and consumed by ch10's epilogue benchmarks and core/common/tcgen05) gets numerically wrong output whenever bias != 0 — the epilogue-fusion 'optimized' variant silently computes a different function than its baseline, so its benchmark comparison is apples-to-oranges as well.

SUGGESTED FIX

Compute each fragment element's global N coordinate from the t2r partition (e.g. build a partitioned coordinate/identity tensor tDgCoord = thr_t2r_copy.partition_D(make_identity_tensor(shape(gD))) and use get<1>(tDgCoord(i)) + tile offset to index bias_ptr), then set x = acc_val + bias_ptr[global_n]. Until then, make the function TORCH_CHECK-fail or fall back to an unfused bias add on the output rather than silently dropping the bias.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: host wrapper (lines 309-423) validates bias length == n, converts to fp32, and passes bias_contig.data_ptr with fuse_bias_silu=true, but grep shows bias_ptr is only tested for null at line 166 and never dereferenced — lines 174-179 set x = acc_val ('bias application would need proper coordinate mapping') and apply SiLU only. So the exported function silently drops the bias. The apples-to-oranges benchmark claim also holds: ch10/baseline_matmul_tcgen05_epilogue.py line 89 does C.add_(self.bias) while the optimized path calls the fused kernel (via the identical code copied into ch10/matmul_tcgen05.cu line 312), so baseline and 'optimized' compute different functions with a randn bias. High is right: an exported PYBIND11 API returning numerically wrong results for any nonzero bias.

sections:
PROBLEM

run_vllm_routing_with_topology maintains only tpot_ema (tokens emitted per step, a throughput number) and passes it as BOTH arguments of snapshot_metrics; snapshot_metrics (line 234, 241-243) maps ttft_ema directly to the router's 'ttft_ms' key. Router.default_scoring_fn (router_policy.py lines 134-143) computes inv_ttft = 1/(1+ttft_ms) with weight 1.5 for prefill scoring, so a GPU that emits MORE tokens per step gets a LOWER prefill score and the 'optimized' router steers new requests away from the fastest GPU. The parallel dual-pool loop (line 724) shows the correct call with a separate ttft_ema dict, proving this is a wiring mistake, not a design choice. Additionally 'tokens' (line 220, sum of len(o.token_ids) over cumulative vLLM RequestOutputs) over-counts per-step tokens, further inflating the value being misused as latency.

EVIDENCE
router.update_metrics(gid, eng.snapshot_metrics(ttft_ema=tpot_ema[gid], tpot_ema=tpot_ema[gid]))

SUGGESTED FIX

Maintain a separate TTFT EMA from the ttft_new samples already collected in the loop (as done at lines ~703-724 for the dual-pool path) and pass it as ttft_ema: eng.snapshot_metrics(ttft_ema=ttft_ema[gid], tpot_ema=tpot_ema[gid]); also compute per-step token deltas instead of summing cumulative token_ids.

VERIFIER NOTES

Line 526 passes tpot_ema as both ttft_ema and tpot_ema; snapshot_metrics (lines 234, 242) maps ttft_ema straight to 'ttft_ms'; router_policy.default_scoring_fn computes inv_ttft=1/(1+ttft_ms) weighted 1.5 for prefill. The dual-pool loop (lines 702-724) maintains a separate ttft_ema and passes it correctly, confirming a wiring mistake. The token over-count claim also holds: line 220 sums len(o.token_ids) over vLLM's cumulative CompletionOutputs each step. One nuance: the 'steers away from the fastest GPU' direction only holds for tpot < ~0.73 (the +0.5*tpot term dominates above that); the more accurate statement is that the TTFT signal is replaced by garbage that flattens inv_ttft toward 0. The optimized routing arm of the demo is still scored on a wrong metric, so high stands.

In the optimized multi-node path with overlap_mode='local_remote' (the default for the optimized entrypoint, line 1255), the remote _roundtrip_routes runs inside 'with torch.cuda.stream(self._comm_stream)' (line 871) while the same-rank _apply_local_experts and the same-node _roundtrip_routes (lines 893-916) are enqueued afterwards on the default stream, with no inter-stream sync until current_stream.wait_stream(self._comm_stream) at line 943. Both branches allocate their working tensors from the same cache: _buffer() keys on (name, device, dtype) only (line 386: 'key = (name, target_device, dtype)') and returns 'cached[:numel].view(shape)' whenever the cached storage is large enough. The remote branch and the same-node branch both request labels "recv_tokens", "recv_weights", "recv_meta", "route_meta", "return_tokens" (and _apply_local_experts requests "local_outputs"/"local_sorted_outputs") with reuse=True. After the first couple of steps the cached storage is >= both requests, so the same-node all_to_all and expert GEMMs on the default stream write the very storage the in-flight remote all_to_all/expert compute on the comm stream is still reading/writing — a silent data race that corrupts remote expert outputs (and hence loss/gradients) precisely in the flagship 'overlap' configuration on multi-node runs.

EVIDENCE
recv_tokens = self._all_to_all_single(sorted_tokens, send_counts, recv_counts, group=group, label="recv_tokens", reuse=reuse)
... (remote call at line 873 under `with torch.cuda.stream(self._comm_stream):`; same-node call at lines 903-915 on the default stream with reuse=True; _buffer key at line 386: `key = (name, target_device, dtype)`)

SUGGESTED FIX

Namespace the buffer cache per branch/stream — e.g. include the event_label ("remote"/"same_node"/"local") in the _buffer key, or pass distinct labels ("remote.recv_tokens" vs "same_node.recv_tokens", and separate local_outputs labels per call site) — so concurrent branches never alias storage. Also record_stream() or event-sync any tensor produced on the comm stream before default-stream code may reuse its storage.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: _buffer keys on (name, target_device, dtype) only (line 386) and returns cached[:numel].view(shape). The remote _roundtrip_routes runs under 'with torch.cuda.stream(self._comm_stream)' (871-885) and requests labels route_meta/recv_tokens/recv_weights/recv_meta/return_tokens with reuse=True (lines 717-744), plus local_outputs/local_sorted_outputs inside _apply_local_experts (558-574, reuse=self.optimized). The same-rank experts (893-897) and same-node roundtrip (903-915) then request the exact same labels on the default stream, same dtypes/device, so once the cache is large enough for both, storage aliases. The only cross-stream syncs are comm_stream.wait_stream(current) at 870 (wrong direction for this hazard) and current_stream.wait_stream(comm) at 943 — after the aliased default-stream work. Blocking host copies inside the roundtrips sync host-to-stream only, not stream-to-stream. overlap_mode defaults to 'local_remote' for the optimized entrypoint (line 1255). High is correct (multi-node optimized path, silent corruption).

The harness coerces the tuple as (rtol, atol) (core/benchmark/verification_mixin.py:90 `ToleranceSpec(rtol=float(tolerance[0]), atol=float(tolerance[1]))`), so this payload allows |actual - ref| <= 10.0 + 1.0*|ref|. The verified output is a slice of cache_k/cache_v — K/V projections of LayerNormed inputs, values O(1) — so ANY tensor whose entries are <= ~10 in magnitude passes, including an all-zero cache or completely wrong quantization. The baseline (baseline_kv_cache.py:244) uses the same vacuous tuple. The FP8-vs-NVFP4 comparison this lab exists for can therefore never fail verification, masking any real TE/NVFP4 numerics bug (which is exactly what a block-scaling regression would look like).

EVIDENCE
            output_tolerance=(1.0, 10.0),

SUGGESTED FIX

Use a tolerance calibrated to the actual FP8->NVFP4 delta on these O(1) activations, e.g. output_tolerance=(0.1, 0.05) (NVFP4 block quantization error on the projection GEMMs is a few percent), in both baseline_kv_cache.py:244 and optimized_kv_cache_nvfp4.py:79; verify against a BF16 (unquantized) reference rather than FP8-vs-NVFP4 if a tighter bound is wanted.

VERIFIER NOTES

verification_mixin.py:90 (_coerce_tolerance) confirms the tuple maps to ToleranceSpec(rtol=tolerance[0], atol=tolerance[1]), so (1.0, 10.0) → rtol=1.0, atol=10.0. With rtol=1.0 an all-zero output passes for ANY reference magnitude, since |0 - ref| = |ref| <= 10 + 1.0*|ref| is always true — the check is mathematically vacuous, not merely loose, independent of the O(1) activation-scale argument. The verified output (_build_verification_output, baseline_kv_cache.py:206-225) is a slice of cache_k/cache_v. Same vacuous tuple at baseline_kv_cache.py:244 and optimized_kv_cache_nvfp4.py:79. The lab's FP8-vs-NVFP4 output verification can never fail (except NaN).

Transformer Engine's recipe classes are dataclasses; NVFP4BlockScaling's documented/actual parameters are e.g. disable_rht / disable_2d_quantization (see TE docs and this repo's own usages: core/benchmark/nvfp4_mlp.py:104 `te_recipe.NVFP4BlockScaling()` and ch13/optimized_fp4_perchannel.py:130 `NVFP4BlockScaling(disable_rht=True, disable_stochastic_rounding=True)`). `calibration_steps`, `amax_history_len`, and `fp4_tensor_block` are not fields (amax history belongs to DelayedScaling; the NVFP4 block size of 16 is fixed by hardware, not a kwarg). Because this constructor runs in __init__ whenever TE_AVAILABLE, OptimizedKVCacheNVFP4Benchmark() raises `TypeError: __init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'calibration_steps'` on exactly the B200/TE machines the lab targets, before setup() can even run.

EVIDENCE
            te_recipe.NVFP4BlockScaling(calibration_steps=20, amax_history_len=16, fp4_tensor_block=16)

SUGGESTED FIX

Construct the recipe as `te_recipe.NVFP4BlockScaling()` (optionally with real fields such as disable_rht/disable_stochastic_rounding), matching core/benchmark/nvfp4_mlp.py:104; calibration is already handled separately via te_autocast(calibrating=True) in _calibrate_fp8(). The identical bogus call in ch19/optimized_nvfp4_training.py:94 should be fixed the same way.

VERIFIER NOTES

The repo vendors TE at third_party/TransformerEngine; transformer_engine/common/recipe/__init__.py:387 defines NVFP4BlockScaling as a @dataclass whose only fields are disable_rht, disable_stochastic_rounding, disable_2d_quantization, fp4_format, fp8_format, fp8_dpa, fp8_mha — no calibration_steps, amax_history_len, or fp4_tensor_block (amax_history_len belongs to DelayedScaling, line 121). A dataclass __init__ raises TypeError on unknown kwargs, and the call runs unconditionally in __init__ whenever TE_AVAILABLE, so OptimizedKVCacheNVFP4Benchmark() crashes before setup() on every TE-equipped machine; without TE the target is skipped. The optimized target therefore can never run anywhere — same 'can never complete' class as the gemv NameError finding, so I raise severity to high (loud failure, but total). The identical bogus call exists at ch19/optimized_nvfp4_training.py:94; correct usages exist at core/benchmark/nvfp4_mlp.py:104 and third_party TE tests.

GroupedMoEExperts.forward copies the expert offsets/counts tensor from GPU into a pinned host buffer with non_blocking=True (pin_memory is set at line 148, so the copy is genuinely asynchronous), then immediately reads the host values in the per-expert loop ('count = int(expert_counts_cpu[expert_id])', line 293; 'start = int(expert_offsets_cpu[expert_id])', line 296) with no torch.cuda.synchronize()/event sync in between. int() on a CPU tensor does not synchronize CUDA. If the copy has not landed, the loop reads stale or uninitialized torch.empty garbage, so expert segment boundaries are wrong: tokens get sliced into the wrong expert's GEMM (silently wrong output, since Python slicing clamps out-of-range bounds) or experts are skipped entirely. This is the Level4Triton benchmark's actual compute path.

EVIDENCE
expert_metadata_host.copy_(expert_metadata, non_blocking=expert_counts.device.type == "cuda")
        expert_offsets_cpu = expert_metadata_host[0]
        expert_counts_cpu = expert_metadata_host[1]
...
        for expert_id in range(self.num_experts):
            count = int(expert_counts_cpu[expert_id])

SUGGESTED FIX

Synchronize before reading the host buffer: record a torch.cuda.Event after the copy_ and call event.synchronize() (or torch.cuda.current_stream().synchronize()) before the 'for expert_id in range(...)' loop; alternatively drop non_blocking (pass non_blocking=False), which makes the D2H copy blocking.

VERIFIER NOTES

Evidence exact: line 285 copies to a pinned host buffer (pin_memory=True at line 148) with non_blocking=True, and lines 293/296 read it via int() with no event/stream sync anywhere in forward(); int() on a CPU tensor does not sync CUDA, so the race is real and the first forward reads torch.empty garbage. Severity downgraded from critical: Level4Triton's routing is deterministic per iteration (fixed input_ids through the same gate), so once the first copy lands, stale reads return identical values — measured iterations and verification capture (after setup's warmup + synchronize at line ~480) are correct in practice; only early warmup forwards compute garbage. The bug would be silently wrong under any dynamic routing, so the fix is still warranted.

memory_budget, moe_grouping, network_affinity, parallelism_breakdown, and pipeline_schedule all use gpt_cluster (GB200 NVL72 preset: 72 nodes x 8 GPUs = 576, 192 GB HBM) but their plans multiply out to 128 GPUs (e.g. optimized dp=4,pp=4,tp=2,ep=4). Verified by running the planner: every one of these scenarios — including the 'optimized' arm — reports 'World size 128 does not match available GPUs 576' and 'Stage GPU count 36.0 does not match TP×EP grid 8', so the lab's own evaluator flags its recommended plans as invalid. The scenario notes also carry stale DGX-A100 facts contradicting the attached cluster: '...blows past 80 GB' (line 58, cluster has 192 GB), 'only 64 ranks assigned to a 128 GPU cluster' (line 196, cluster has 576), and '4 DP replicas fully tile the 16 nodes' (line 217, cluster has 72 nodes).

EVIDENCE
"4 DP replicas fully tile the 16 nodes, keeping optimizer sharding localized",

SUGGESTED FIX

Either bind these five scenarios to the dgx_a100_175b preset (SPEC_PRESETS['dgx_a100_175b'], 16x8=128 GPUs, 80 GB, HDR100 — which every plan size and note was written for), or rescale each plan's dp/pp/tp/ep to factor 576 and rewrite the notes for GB200 (192 GB HBM, 800G CX8, 72 nodes).

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified by inspection and by running the planner: gpt_cluster is SPEC_PRESETS['gpt_oss_120b_gb200_ib'] (72x8=576 GPUs, 192 GB); memory_budget, moe_grouping, network_affinity, parallelism_breakdown, and pipeline_schedule plans all factor to 128 (or 64) GPUs, and every arm — including each 'optimized' recommendation — emits 'World size 128 does not match available GPUs 576' and 'Stage GPU count 36.0 does not match TP×EP grid 8' hotspots. The stale DGX-A100 notes are present exactly as cited: 'blows past 80 GB' (line 58), 'only 64 ranks assigned to a 128 GPU cluster' (line 196), '4 DP replicas fully tile the 16 nodes' (line 217). The dgx_a100_175b preset (16x8=128, 80 GB, HDR100) exists and matches every plan size, supporting the mis-binding theory.

PROBLEM

_decode_forward_step runs the entire model forward inside 'with torch.cuda.stream(self._persistent_stream)' and returns logits with no event/wait_stream in either direction ('Synchronize only if needed (caller will handle this in most cases)'). No caller handles it: generate() immediately does 'logits = logits[:, -1, :]' and sample_next_token(...) on the default stream (lines 1069-1077), so sampling kernels can read logits before the forward on the persistent stream has written them; symmetrically, the persistent stream reads ids that were written on the default stream without waiting for it. Result: nondeterministically wrong logits/tokens whenever enable_persistent_decode=True (exercised by scripts/bench_b200_flags.py mode 'persistent' and benchmark_incremental_optimizations.py). Additionally logits are allocated on the side stream and consumed/freed relative to the default stream without record_stream(), an allocator-reuse hazard.

EVIDENCE
if self.enable_persistent_decode and self._persistent_stream is not None:
            # Run decode in dedicated stream to allow better kernel pipelining
            # and overlap with CPU operations (e.g., sampling, token processing)
            with torch.cuda.stream(self._persistent_stream):
                logits = self.model.forward(ids, kv_cache=kv_cache, attention_mask=attention_mask, token_mask=token_mask)
            # Synchronize only if needed (caller will handle this in most cases)
            return logits

SUGGESTED FIX

Before entering the side stream do self._persistent_stream.wait_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream()); after the forward, record an event on the persistent stream and make the current stream wait on it before returning (and call logits.record_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream())). Or drop the side stream: a single serialized decode step gains nothing from a second stream, so the honest fix is to remove the block.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: lines 488-494 run model.forward inside torch.cuda.stream(self._persistent_stream) and return logits with no event/wait in either direction. A grep of engine.py finds no wait_stream or record_stream anywhere; the only torch.cuda.synchronize calls are in _capture_decode_graph (559) and the __main__ bench section (1350+). generate() consumes the logits immediately on the default stream (lines 1069-1078: slice + sample_next_token). The stream is created whenever enable_persistent_decode=True and use_cuda_graphs=False (lines 410-422), which is exactly bench_b200_flags.py mode 'persistent'. Both the read-before-write race and the allocator-reuse hazard (no record_stream) are real. High is correct.

_decode_forward_step runs the entire model forward inside 'with torch.cuda.stream(self._persistent_stream)' and returns logits with no event/wait_stream in either direction ('Synchronize only if needed (caller will handle this in most cases)'). No caller handles it: generate() immediately does 'logits = logits[:, -1, :]' and sample_next_token(...) on the default stream (lines 1069-1077), so sampling kernels can read logits before the forward on the persistent stream has written them; symmetrically, the persistent stream reads ids that were written on the default stream without waiting for it. Result: nondeterministically wrong logits/tokens whenever enable_persistent_decode=True (exercised by scripts/bench_b200_flags.py mode 'persistent' and benchmark_incremental_optimizations.py). Additionally logits are allocated on the side stream and consumed/freed relative to the default stream without record_stream(), an allocator-reuse hazard.

if self.enable_persistent_decode and self._persistent_stream is not None:
            # Run decode in dedicated stream to allow better kernel pipelining
            # and overlap with CPU operations (e.g., sampling, token processing)
            with torch.cuda.stream(self._persistent_stream):
                logits = self.model.forward(ids, kv_cache=kv_cache, attention_mask=attention_mask, token_mask=token_mask)
            # Synchronize only if needed (caller will handle this in most cases)
            return logits
SUGGESTED FIX

Before entering the side stream do self._persistent_stream.wait_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream()); after the forward, record an event on the persistent stream and make the current stream wait on it before returning (and call logits.record_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream())). VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: lines 488-494 run model.forward inside torch.cuda.stream(self._persistent_stream) and return logits with no event/wait in either direction. _token_tensor_to_list copies sampled token ids from GPU into a pinned host buffer with non_blocking=True and immediately calls .tolist() on it. A non-blocking device-to-pinned-host copy returns before the DMA completes and .tolist() on a CPU tensor performs no CUDA synchronization, so the host can read stale tokens from the previous step or uninitialized garbage. The same pattern appears at lines 992-993 ('sampled_host.copy_(sampled_device, non_blocking=...); next_tokens = sampled_host.tolist()'). _sample_host_token_buffer explicitly pins the buffer when the source is CUDA (lines 820-832), which is exactly the condition under which the copy is truly asynchronous. These token ids drive generation state (completion checks, tool-use parsing, forced tokens), so a lost race silently corrupts generated text; because small copies usually finish within microseconds it manifests as a rare, unreproducible wrong-token heisenbug.

EVIDENCE
host_tokens = self._sample_host_token_buffer(flat_tokens.numel(), flat_tokens.device)
        host_tokens.copy_(flat_tokens, non_blocking=flat_tokens.device.type == "cuda")
        return host_tokens.tolist()

SUGGESTED FIX

After the copy_, synchronize before reading: torch.cuda.current_stream(flat_tokens.device).synchronize() (or record an event and event.synchronize()), or simply use non_blocking=False for these tiny D2H copies — the transfer is a few hundred bytes and the async form buys nothing while introducing the race. Apply the same fix at lines 992-993.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: _token_tensor_to_list (916-920) does host_tokens.copy_(flat_tokens, non_blocking=True-when-CUDA) then .tolist() immediately; _sample_host_token_buffer pins the buffer exactly when the source is CUDA (820-832), which is the condition making the copy truly asynchronous. The same pattern repeats at 992-993. No stream/event sync exists between the copy and the host read (grep confirms), and nothing upstream (multinomial/argmax with device generator) forces a sync. This is the canonical non_blocking D2H race PyTorch's own docs warn about, and the tokens feed completion checks, tool-use parsing, and the yielded text. Executes every decode step, so a per-step-rare race compounds over a generation; high is defensible.

_time_cuda_region_seconds records start/end CUDA events on torch.cuda.current_stream() (lines 21-25) around _run_decode. In mode 'persistent' (config.enable_persistent_decode=True, line 76), the loop calls engine._execute_decode, which launches the model forward on engine._persistent_stream (engine.py line 491) — a different stream. The end event recorded on the default stream does not wait for the persistent stream, so end.synchronize() completes after only the Python launch overhead; the actual decode kernels are excluded from the measured window. The reported decode_tok_s for the 'persistent' row is therefore enormously inflated — a multi-stream timing exploit of exactly the kind the repo's own harness guards against with full_device_sync — and the script's purpose ('see the incremental benefit on Blackwell') is defeated for the one flag it was written to evaluate.

SUGGESTED FIX

Time with a full device sync: in _time_cuda_region_seconds, replace end.synchronize() with torch.cuda.synchronize() before reading elapsed_time, or record the end event on engine._persistent_stream when an engine is in use (after making the default stream wait on it). Wall-clock + torch.cuda.synchronize() around the region is the simplest correct form.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: _time_cuda_region_seconds (18-26) records start/end on torch.cuda.current_stream() and syncs only the end event. Mode 'persistent' sets config.enable_persistent_decode=True (76), run_benchmark then constructs an Engine (142-143), and _run_decode calls engine._execute_decode (125), which launches the forward on engine._persistent_stream (engine.py 491) since use_cuda_graphs is False. The end event on the default stream has no dependency on the side stream, so the measured window covers launch overhead only and the 'persistent' decode_tok_s row is inflated — for the one flag the script exists to evaluate. High is correct.
