sections:
PROBLEM

With H=4096 unit-normal inputs and weights, gate = x@W1 has std ~64, and after SiLU*up the hidden values have magnitudes on the order of 64*64 ~= 4096 — far beyond float8_e4m3fn's max of 448. 'hidden_fp8_slice.copy_(gate)' with self.scale = torch.ones(()) (line 97) therefore saturates the majority of hidden activations to +/-448, so the third GEMM computes numerically meaningless outputs; the header's 'FP8: 55-58% of peak -> 1.4x speedup!' compares timing of garbage math against real math. Separately, get_extra_metrics reports 'b200_peak_tflops': 2250 — the BF16 dense peak — for an FP8 workload (FP8 dense peak is ~2x higher), roughly doubling the claimed percent-of-peak. The forward also never unsorts or top-k-combines: self.output stays [batch*K, H] in expert-sorted assignment order, so it is not an MoE layer output.

EVIDENCE
hidden_fp8_slice.copy_(gate)

SUGGESTED FIX

Use per-tensor (or per-token) amax-based scaling for the activation quantization (scale_a = amax/448 computed from gate before the copy, passed to _scaled_mm), report utilization against the FP8 peak (~4500 dense TFLOPS for B200) in get_extra_metrics, and add the unsort + top-k weighted combine so the benchmark computes an actual MoE forward.

VERIFIER NOTES

All three claims verified. self.scale=torch.ones(()) (line 97) and hidden_fp8_slice.copy_(gate) (line 195): with H=4096 unit-normal x and w1/w3, gate/up have std ~64, so silu(gate)*up magnitudes are on the order of thousands, far past e4m3fn's 448 max — most values saturate (or map to NaN, since PyTorch's e4m3fn overflow maps to NaN), making the third _scaled_mm meaningless while the header claims '55-58% of peak -> 1.4x speedup'. get_extra_metrics (line 230) reports b200_peak_tflops=2250, the BF16 dense figure, for an FP8 workload (~2x the correct denominator). And benchmark_fn writes weighted outputs into sorted [batch*K, H] positions (line 203) with no unsort or top-k combine.

sections:
PROBLEM

fused_moe_expert_kernel never tiles the intermediate dimension in the first matmul: offs_n = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N) (line 68) is fixed, so gate_acc/up_acc cover only intermediate columns 0..63 of I=11008. The second matmul then loops n over I but slices 'hidden[:, n:n+BLOCK_N]' — hidden is a [BLOCK_M, 64] register tile, so every n>0 slice is out of bounds (and start:stop slicing of a Triton tensor is not supported, so the kernel fails to compile in practice, caught by the bare try/except which prints 'Triton kernel failed'). The store (lines 114-116) writes only offs_k = 0..63 of the H=4096 output columns, leaving the rest of the torch.empty_like output uninitialized, and no top-k combine is performed. Despite this, benchmark_triton_moe computes flops = batch_seq*K*3*2*H*I (line 227) and prints 'TFLOPS ({tflops/2250*100:.1f}%)' as though three full GEMMs ran — a misleading benchmark claim off by roughly I/BLOCK_N x H/BLOCK_K.

EVIDENCE
h_block = hidden[:, n:n+BLOCK_N]

SUGGESTED FIX

Rewrite the kernel to tile the N (intermediate) dimension as a proper grid axis or inner loop that recomputes/stores hidden per N-tile, accumulate the down-projection across all N tiles, and loop/store over the full H output dimension; or delete the kernel and route the demo through the working grouped path. Until the kernel computes the counted FLOPs, remove the TFLOPS/percent-of-peak print.

VERIFIER NOTES

All code claims verified: offs_n fixed at tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N) (line 68) so the first matmul only covers intermediate columns 0..63 of I=11008; line 102 slices hidden[:, n:n+BLOCK_N] — start:stop slicing of a Triton tensor is unsupported, so the kernel fails to compile and the bare try/except (lines 202-235) prints the failure; the store (lines 114-116) covers only 64 of 4096 output columns; flops at line 227 counts three full GEMMs. Severity downgraded from high: because compilation fails loudly with a traceback, the misleading 'TFLOPS (% of peak)' line 230 is unreachable in practice — the shipped defect is a broken 'holy grail' kernel, not a live inflated benchmark number.

sections:
PROBLEM

fused_expert_ffn_kernel's second matmul loops n over the full intermediate dim N but always multiplies the SAME first-BLOCK_N hidden tile ('out_acc += tl.dot(hidden...)'), because only intermediate columns 0..BLOCK_N-1 were ever computed; the hidden_slice at lines 136-139 is an unused placeholder with the comment 'Would need to store/reload hidden - simplified here'. For any N > BLOCK_N the result is mathematically wrong (sum over n of hidden_block0 @ W2[n_block] instead of the true contraction). grouped_gemm_kernel (lines 148-207) is worse: a_ptr/c_ptr are never offset by the group's row start (lines 197, 206 use only rm/rn), so every 'group' reads the same A rows and all groups scatter into the same C tile, overwriting each other. Neither kernel is launched by any benchmark, but both are shipped in a book lab as 'the pattern used by CUTLASS grouped GEMM for MoE'.

EVIDENCE
out_acc += tl.dot(hidden.to(tl.float32), w2_slice.to(tl.float32))

SUGGESTED FIX

Fix fused_expert_ffn_kernel by tiling N properly (compute hidden per N-tile inside the second loop, or restructure as two passes with a staging buffer) and fix grouped_gemm_kernel by loading a per-group row offset (prefix-sum of group sizes) and adding 'group_start * stride_am' / 'group_start * stride_cm' to the A/C pointers with per-group M in the masks — or delete both kernels since the lab never calls them.

VERIFIER NOTES

Both defects verified. fused_expert_ffn_kernel: rn is fixed at tl.arange(0, BLOCK_N) (line 83), so gate_acc/up_acc only cover intermediate columns 0..BLOCK_N-1; the second loop (lines 127-140) multiplies the same 'hidden' tile against every W2 n-block (line 140), with hidden_slice (lines 136-139) an unused placeholder whose own comment admits the simplification — mathematically wrong for any N > BLOCK_N (and the runtime-conditional 'if n_start == 0' would not even compile in a dynamic Triton loop). grouped_gemm_kernel: a/c pointer arithmetic (lines 197, 206) uses only rm/rn with no per-group row base, so all groups read the same A rows and overwrite the same C tile. Repo-wide grep confirms neither kernel is imported or launched anywhere (level4_triton.py defines a separate, distinct grouped_gemm_kernel), so the harm is confined to shipped teaching content presenting broken patterns.

sections:
PROBLEM

ep_bytes multiplies by max(plan.ep - 1, 1): with ep=1 there is no expert-parallel all-to-all at all, yet the model charges a full hop of traffic (and moe_tokens_per_gpu is then the entire routed token count), inflating estimated_step_ms for every EP=1 plan and biasing plan comparisons toward EP>1. Separately, the hotspot strings 'Expert groups span nodes, forcing HDR100 all-to-all traffic' (line 427) and 'Pipeline activation transfers saturate HDR100' (line 435) hardcode the DGX-A100 HDR100 NIC name; verified by running the planner: the gpt_gb200 and deepseek_gb200 scenarios (dual 800G CX8 InfiniBand) print 'Pipeline activation transfers saturate HDR100' in their reports — a wrong hardware claim in the lab's output.

SUGGESTED FIX

Change the multiplier to max(plan.ep - 1, 0) so EP=1 incurs zero EP communication (and ideally use the (ep-1)/ep fraction of per-GPU routed bytes), and derive the NIC name in hotspot strings from cluster.name/cluster.interconnect (e.g. f"saturate {cluster.interconnect} NICs") instead of the hardcoded 'HDR100'.

VERIFIER NOTES

Both sub-claims verified. ep_bytes (lines 374-380) multiplies by max(plan.ep - 1, 1), so EP=1 plans are charged a full hop of all-to-all traffic that does not exist (and moe_tokens_per_gpu at line 323 is then the full routed token count), inflating estimated_step_ms and biasing comparisons. Hotspot strings at lines 427 and 435 hardcode 'HDR100'; running the planner shows gpt_gb200 and deepseek_gb200 (GB200, dual 800G CX8) printing 'Pipeline activation transfers saturate HDR100' — a wrong hardware name in the lab's own output.

sections:
PROBLEM

benchmark_inference times prefill/decode by calling the model directly ('_ = model(step_ids, kv_cache=kv_cache)'); it never constructs an Engine. But enable_persistent_decode and use_cuda_graphs are consumed only by the Engine (gpt.py lines 84-85: 'gate persistent decode kernels (Engine)', 'gate CUDA Graph capture in Engine generate paths'; engine.py lines 364-365 read them via model.config). So the configs named '+ enable_persistent_decode' (line 275) and '+ use_cuda_graphs' (line 294) run byte-identical GPU work to the preceding row, and any 'incremental benefit' printed for those rows (improvement_vs_baseline / cumulative_improvement) is pure run-to-run noise presented as an optimization result — a fabricated benchmark claim for two of the lab's headline features.

SUGGESTED FIX

For the persistent-decode and cuda-graphs rows, build an Engine(model, tokenizer) and drive decode through engine._execute_decode (with device-synchronized timing per the bench_b200_flags fix), or drop those two rows from this script and state that they are Engine-level features not measurable via direct model calls.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: benchmark_inference imports only KVCache and calls model(...) directly for prefill and decode (lines 132-134, 142-167); no Engine is ever constructed in the script. A repo grep shows enable_persistent_decode and use_cuda_graphs appear outside engine.py only as GPTConfig field declarations (gpt.py 84-85, commented 'gate ... (Engine)'); nothing in the model forward reads them. So the '+ enable_persistent_decode' (line 275) and '+ use_cuda_graphs' (line 294) rows run GPU work identical to the preceding row and their printed improvements are run-to-run noise. Medium is correct.

sections:
PROBLEM

The 'baseline' wrapper passes custom_kernel=custom_kernel_custom_cuda (the hand-written tcgen05 kernel) with slower env tuning, and optimized_nvfp4_group_gemm.py wraps the identical kernel with faster tuning. The harness A/B verification (output_tolerance=(1e-3,1e-3) in nvfp4_group_gemm_common.py:308) therefore compares the custom kernel against itself; grep confirms no torch._scaled_mm or any independent reference implementation exists anywhere in this lab. A systematic numerics bug shared by both configurations (e.g. a scale-factor layout error in _pack_scale_tiles_for_tcgen05 or in the .cu kernel that both configs consume identically) produces identical wrong outputs in both targets and passes 'verification' cleanly.

EVIDENCE
        custom_kernel=custom_kernel_custom_cuda,

SUGGESTED FIX

Add an independent reference check: in NVFP4GroupGemmBenchmark.setup() (or a verify-only path), compute each group's expected output with torch._scaled_mm using the unreordered sfa/sfb (as the GPU MODE reference does, cf. labs/nvfp4_gemm/reference_submission.py ref_kernel) and assert the custom kernel matches within (1e-3, 1e-3) before timing.

With input_scale=1e-3 and k=4096, output elements of C have std ~= 2.1e-5 and max ~= 1.2e-4, so atol=1e-2 (from get_output_tolerance() -> (1e-2, 1e-2) in baseline_ozaki_scheme.py:71 and optimized_ozaki_scheme_dynamic.py:112) is ~100x larger than the LARGEST output element. Moreover the harness verifies only a single float32 signed checksum per binary (CudaBinaryBenchmark returns torch.tensor([self._verify_checksum])), in which sign-random per-element errors cancel. The kernel maps exactly one program to one work item (`pid` indexes work_seq_ids directly, line 37 comment: "one program per sequence") and the launch caps the item count at `self._num_items = min(self.batch, self.num_programs)`. There is no grid-stride loop and no device-side work queue — the `work_counter` tensor built by build_inputs() is never passed to the kernel. The right-sized target exposes `--num-programs` as a CLI override (optimized_right_sized_decode.py line 27); e.g. `--tier large --num-programs 8` gives batch=12 but processes only sequences 0-7, leaving out[8:12] as zeros. validate_result() only checks isfinite, so the benchmark passes while computing 2/3 of the workload, and tokens_per_iteration still reports batch*seq_len — the measured speedup is inflated by silently skipped work. The docstring "Persistent decode in Triton with a device-side work queue" is contradicted by the code.

EVIDENCE
Line 83: `self._num_items = min(self.batch, self.num_programs)`; kernel line 37-41: `pid = tl.program_id(0)  # one program per sequence` / `if pid >= num_items: return` / `seq_id = tl.load(work_seq_ids_ptr + pid)` — no loop over remaining items and work_counter unused.

SUGGESTED FIX

Grid-stride over work items inside the kernel (like persistent_decode_ext.cu does: `for seq = pid; seq < num_items; seq += tl.num_programs(0)`), and pass batch as num_items instead of min(batch, num_programs); or raise an error when num_programs < batch.

VERIFIER NOTES

Evidence verified: line 83 `_num_items = min(self.batch, self.num_programs)`, grid = (_num_items,), kernel maps pid directly to one sequence (lines 37-41) with no grid-stride loop, and work_counter (persistent_decode_common.py line 135) is never passed — the 'device-side work queue' docstring (line 1) is false. --num-programs is exposed (optimized_right_sized_decode.py line 27); with it below batch, out[batch_drop:] stays zeros while validate_result checks only isfinite (lines 187-192) and the verification view covers only out[:1,:8], so the drop is silent and tokens_per_iteration still reports batch*seq_len. Downgraded to medium: every default tier sets num_programs == batch (small 4/4, medium 8/8, large 12/12), so the drop occurs only under an explicit CLI override — though the lab invites exactly that sweep.

_copy_to_device() issues `copy_(..., non_blocking=self.cfg.use_pinned_stage)` from the shared CPU staging tensor, and benchmark_fn()'s repeat_pages loop then calls _stage_page(start) for the next page, which host-writes the same `self.staging` buffer (`target[..., :slice_len, :].copy_(self._host_page_view(...))`, lines 251-253). Nothing on the host waits for the previously enqueued async DMA read of that buffer: with copy_stream=None the "wait_for_copy" branch does nothing, and the only sync primitives (`consumer_stream.wait_stream`, `prefetch_event`) order GPU streams, not the CPU thread. In optimized_paged_kv_offload.py (use_pinned_stage=True, use_memmap=True so the direct-view shortcut is disabled, repeat_pages=32), the CPU can overwrite pinned staging while the DMA for the previous page is still reading it, silently corrupting the KV page consumed by F.scaled_dot_product_attention and producing nondeterministic outputs/verification mismatches. The same reuse race applies to prefetch_staging in the async two-buffer path.

EVIDENCE
Lines 276-279: `target_kv[..., :slice_len, :].copy_(staged[..., :slice_len, :], non_blocking=self.cfg.use_pinned_stage,)` and lines 251-253: `target[..., :slice_len, :].copy_(self._host_page_view(start, slice_len))` — executed per loop iteration in benchmark_fn (lines 535-542) with no host-side cudaEvent/stream synchronize before the staging buffer is rewritten.

SUGGESTED FIX

Record a cuda Event after each staging-sourced H2D copy and call event.synchronize() (or torch.cuda.current_stream().synchronize()) before the next _stage_page() writes that staging buffer; or double-buffer the staging tensors so writes never target a buffer with an in-flight copy.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: _copy_to_device issues copy_(non_blocking=use_pinned_stage) from self.staging (lines 276-289); the wait_for_copy branch (lines 299-301) is inside `if self.copy_stream is not None`, so with use_async_stream=False it does nothing — and even when taken it is a stream-order op, not a host sync. The next repeat_pages iteration host-writes the same pinned staging in _stage_page (lines 251-253) with no event.synchronize() anywhere in the loop (benchmark_fn lines 515-590). optimized_paged_kv_offload.py hits this on its default path: use_pinned_stage=True, use_async_stream=False, use_memmap=True (which forces _host_cache_is_pinned=False, disabling the line-247 direct-view shortcut), repeat_pages=32. One correction: the shipped prefetch target (use_memmap=False, pinned host cache, use_direct_h2d=True) takes the direct-view shortcut, so prefetch_staging is never a copy source there — the 'same race applies to prefetch_staging' aside only holds for non-shipped configs. Medium is right: silent, timing-dependent data corruption in a synthetic benchmark.

The module docstring claims "On Hopper/Blackwell parts with TMA enabled, the compiler lowers these async copies to the TMA engine", and the lab README labels the pair "cp.async vs native TMA scheduling". But the kernel issues `cuda::memcpy_async` of sizeof(float)=4 bytes per thread through a `cuda::pipeline<cuda::thread_scope_thread>`. The TMA engine (cp.async.bulk / cp.async.bulk.tensor) is only reachable via block/cluster-scope bulk copies with an mbarrier and >=16B aligned sizes (or cuTensorMap descriptors); a 4-byte thread-scope memcpy_async lowers to a plain cp.async (LDGSTS) or an ordinary load/store. So optimized_native_tma_prefill_decode.py benchmarks cp.async against cp.async and reports the delta as a native-TMA result — a wrong hardware/API claim in a book about Blackwell TMA.

EVIDENCE
Line 58: `cuda::memcpy_async(&smem[threadIdx.x], &src[global_idx], sizeof(float), pipe);` with line 51: `cuda::pipeline<cuda::thread_scope_thread> pipe = cuda::make_pipeline();` — versus docstring lines 4-6: "On Hopper/Blackwell parts with TMA enabled, the compiler lowers these async copies to the TMA engine."

SUGGESTED FIX

Either implement a real bulk copy (cooperative_groups::memcpy_async at block scope with cuda::barrier and >=16B aligned chunks, or cp.async.bulk.tensor with a cuTensorMap) so TMA is actually engaged, or correct the docstring/README to say the path exercises cp.async (LDGSTS), not the TMA engine.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: line 58 `cuda::memcpy_async(&smem[threadIdx.x], &src[global_idx], sizeof(float), pipe)` with a cuda::thread_scope_thread pipeline (line 51), versus docstring lines 4-6 claiming the compiler lowers these to the TMA engine, and README line 57 labeling the pair 'cp.async vs native TMA scheduling'. Per NVIDIA documentation, TMA (cp.async.bulk / cp.async.bulk.tensor) is reached only via block/cluster-scope bulk copies with an mbarrier and >=16B alignment/size (or cuTensorMap); a 4-byte thread-scope pipeline memcpy_async lowers to cp.async (LDGSTS) or a plain load/store. optimized_native_tma_prefill_decode.py (line 124) calls this tma_copy, so the 'native TMA' benchmark exercises cp.async. The reviewer's NVIDIA-facts are correct; medium fits a wrong hardware/API claim in an educational repo.

The script does hook = getattr(comm_hooks, "batched_reduce_scatter_hook", None) against torch.distributed.algorithms.ddp_comm_hooks.default_hooks and raises 'SKIPPED: PyTorch build missing batched_reduce_scatter_hook' when absent. default_hooks in torch 2.8 (verified in this environment) exposes only allreduce_hook, fp16_compress_hook, bf16_compress_hook (plus _compress_hook); no PyTorch release has ever shipped batched_reduce_scatter_hook. So the 'optimized ZeRO-2' single-GPU demo unconditionally skips on every install, and the error message misattributes it to the user's 'PyTorch build'. Even if the hook existed, the script repeats the multigpu file's bug: ZeroRedundancyOptimizer(overlap_with_ddp=True) plus a manual optimizer.step() (a no-op), and additionally passes gradient_as_bucket_view=True into ZeroRedundancyOptimizer, which is not a ZeRO kwarg and would be forwarded into AdamW defaults.

EVIDENCE
hook = getattr(comm_hooks, "batched_reduce_scatter_hook", None)
    if hook is None:
        raise RuntimeError("SKIPPED: PyTorch build missing batched_reduce_scatter_hook required for optimized ZeRO-2.")
    ddp_model.register_comm_hook(state=dist.group.WORLD, hook=hook)

SUGGESTED FIX

Use the real reduce-scatter/all-gather hook defined in optimized_zero2_multigpu.py (or hook_with_zero_step from torch.distributed.algorithms.ddp_comm_hooks.ddp_zero_hook) instead of the nonexistent batched_reduce_scatter_hook; set overlap_with_ddp=False (keeping manual step) or wire the zero-step hook properly; and remove the invalid gradient_as_bucket_view kwarg from ZeroRedundancyOptimizer.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified in this environment (torch 2.8.0): torch.distributed.algorithms.ddp_comm_hooks.default_hooks exposes only allreduce_hook, fp16_compress_hook, bf16_compress_hook, _compress_hook — no batched_reduce_scatter_hook — so lines 77-79 raise the 'SKIPPED: PyTorch build missing...' RuntimeError on every install, misattributing a nonexistent API to the user's build. Secondary claims also verified: overlap_with_ddp=True plus manual optimizer.step() (lines 87, 106, 123) would be the same no-op as the multigpu file, and ZeroRedundancyOptimizer.__init__'s signature is (params, optimizer_class, process_group, parameters_as_bucket_view, overlap_with_ddp, **defaults), so gradient_as_bucket_view=True (line 88) would be forwarded into AdamW defaults. Medium is correct for a lab that unconditionally self-skips.

format_prometheus() iterates over individual samples and, for every `gpu_memory*` sample, re-emits `# HELP <family>` and `# TYPE <family>` derived from name.split('{')[0]. With more than one GPU (the normal case for this repo's 2x/8x B200 and 4x GB200 targets), the same metric family (e.g. gpu_memory_allocated_gb) gets a second HELP and TYPE line for gpu="1", which the Prometheus text-format parser treats as a fatal error ('second HELP line for metric name') - the entire scrape fails and no metrics are ingested. The exporter works only on single-GPU machines, contradicting its purpose as the repo's cluster monitoring endpoint.

SUGGESTED FIX

Track emitted family names in a set and emit HELP/TYPE once per family (before its first sample), e.g. `family = name.split('{')[0]; if family not in seen: lines += [f'# HELP {family} ...', f'# TYPE {family} gauge']; seen.add(family)`.

test_blackwell_specs is the only CI-gated check on the hardware constants used for roofline/efficiency math, and its bounds are 'hbm_bandwidth_gbps >= 8000', 'num_sms > 100', 'fp8_tflops > 1000'. The constants it blesses in code/core/benchmark/metrics.py are wrong: fp8_tflops=2500.0 is commented 'FP8 Tensor Core sparse' but NVIDIA's B200 FP8 tensor figure is ~4500 TFLOPS dense / ~9000 sparse (DGX B200: 72 PFLOPS FP8 across 8 GPUs), and tensor_tflops=1250.0 (FP16 Tensor Core) vs the published ~2250 TFLOPS dense. Any '% of peak FP8' or tensor-roofline number computed from these constants overstates achieved efficiency by roughly 2x, and the test passes on values off by 2-4x because the threshold is '> 1000'.

EVIDENCE
assert BLACKWELL_B200.fp8_tflops > 1000   (line 49; test also asserts hbm >= 8000.0 at line 47)
code/core/benchmark/metrics.py:57: fp8_tflops=2500.0,             # FP8 Tensor Core sparse

SUGGESTED FIX

Pin the spec test to the published values with tight bounds (e.g. assert BLACKWELL_B200.fp8_tflops == 4500.0 for dense, tensor_tflops == 2250.0, and document dense-vs-sparse in the field name), and correct the constants in core/benchmark/metrics.py to match the datasheet so the test genuinely locks the specs.

VERIFIER NOTES

test_blackwell_specs asserts only hbm >= 8000, num_sms > 100, fp8_tflops > 1000 (lines ~46-49) and is in the CI allowlist. code/core/benchmark/metrics.py:57-58 has fp8_tflops=2500.0 commented 'FP8 Tensor Core sparse' and tensor_tflops=1250.0 (FP16 Tensor Core). NVIDIA's HGX/DGX B200 figures are ~4.5 PFLOPS FP8 dense / ~9 PFLOPS sparse (72 PFLOPS FP8 across 8 GPUs) and ~2.25 PFLOPS FP16 tensor dense — so 2500 'sparse' is wrong under any reading, and the constants understate peak ~1.8x (dense) which inflates any %-of-peak/efficiency figure accordingly. The H100 entry uses sparse datasheet values (1979/989), making the B200 entry inconsistent as well as wrong. The '>1000' bound genuinely blesses values off by 2-4x. BLACKWELL_B200 is also DEFAULT_SPECS, so this feeds default roofline math.

All six assert-free test functions wrap their body in 'try/except Exception as e: print(...)' or return after a printed skip, so torch.compile crashing, the profiler breaking, or the Triton kernel failing to compile all still pass. test_triton_35 launches an add kernel into 'out' and never checks 'out == 2' — a kernel writing garbage passes. test_cuda_130_features only parses torch.version.cuda and prints; it validates no CUDA 13.0 feature. On any host, pytest reports 6 green tests regardless of whether the Blackwell stack works, which contradicts the file docstring 'Blackwell validation suite covering PyTorch 2.10, CUDA 13.0, and Triton 3.5 features.'

SUGGESTED FIX

Remove the try/except-print wrappers (or re-raise after printing), replace prints with assertions (assert torch.allclose(out, x + y) after the Triton launch; assert compiled model output matches eager), and use pytest.skip for the no-CUDA path instead of 'return' so skips are visible.

VERIFIER NOTES

Confirmed: 'except Exception as e: print(f" torch.compile failed: {e}")' at lines 105-106; Triton except-print at 225-226; add_kernel output 'out' never compared to x+y (lines 216-224); test_cuda_130_features (130-156) only parses torch.version.cuda and prints; no-CUDA paths use bare 'return' via ensure_cuda so they report PASS. Minor count quibble: the file has 8 test functions, not 6 — the two distributed ch16 tests DO carry real asserts but silently return without torchrun/2 GPUs, so pytest actually reports 8 green regardless of stack health. The six functions run by main() are assert-free as claimed. Core claim stands.

The checklist says NCCL_NTHREADS is 'the number of CPU threads per GPU for NCCL' with 'default 4', and recommends raising it to 8 or 16. NCCL_NTHREADS is the number of CUDA threads per CUDA block used by NCCL kernels; its default is 512 on modern GPUs and legal values are 64-512, so setting 8 or 16 is invalid and NCCL will warn and ignore it (the CPU-side knob is NCCL_SOCKET_NTHREADS). The same sentence claims NCCL_BUFFSIZE has a 'default 1 MB' and should be raised to 4 MB -- the NCCL default is already 4194304 bytes (4 MiB), so the recommended 'increase' is a no-op. A reader tuning a multinode job from this text would apply broken settings.

EVIDENCE
increase NCCL_NTHREADS, the number of CPU threads per GPU for NCCL, from the default 4 to 8 or 16 to drive higher bandwidth at the cost of more CPU usage. Increase NCCL_BUFFSIZE, the buffer size per GPU, from the default 1 MB to 4 MB or more

SUGGESTED FIX

Correct to: NCCL_NTHREADS = CUDA threads per NCCL block (default 512 on recent GPUs, valid 64-512, rarely needs tuning); NCCL_SOCKET_NTHREADS = CPU helper threads for socket transport (raise for high-bandwidth Ethernet); NCCL_BUFFSIZE default is 4 MiB and can be raised (e.g. 8-16 MiB) for very large messages.

VERIFIER NOTES

Quoted sentence verified at docs/appendix.md:856. Per NCCL documentation, NCCL_NTHREADS is the number of CUDA threads per thread block used by NCCL kernels (default 512 on recent architectures, valid range 64-512, must be a power of two); it is not a CPU-thread count and has no 'default 4' — values 8/16 are out of range and NCCL warns and ignores them. The CPU-side knob is NCCL_SOCKET_NTHREADS, as the reviewer says. NCCL_BUFFSIZE default is 4194304 bytes (4 MiB), not 1 MB, so the doc's recommended 'increase to 4 MB' is a no-op. Both semantics and both defaults in the doc are wrong; medium is appropriate for tuning guidance that produces invalid settings.

PROBLEM

The checklist states 'Hopper and Blackwell introduce cp.async and Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) engines'. cp.async (async copy global->shared) was introduced with Ampere, compute capability 8.0, in CUDA 11 -- it works on A100-class GPUs. Only TMA (cp.async.bulk.tensor) is new with Hopper (sm_90). Readers on Ampere would wrongly conclude the double-buffered cp.async pipeline pattern the paragraph teaches is unavailable to them, and the arch-gating advice at line 551 ('Hopper-and-newer builds keep the optimized path') compounds the error for cp.async-only kernels.

EVIDENCE
Hopper and Blackwell introduce `cp.async` and Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) engines that stream tiles into shared memory without stalling warps.

SUGGESTED FIX

Change to: 'Ampere introduced cp.async for asynchronous global-to-shared copies; Hopper and Blackwell add the Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) engine for bulk tensor transfers.'

VERIFIER NOTES

Quoted sentence verified at docs/appendix.md:539 ('Hopper and Blackwell introduce cp.async and Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) engines'). cp.async (async global-to-shared copy) was introduced with Ampere cc 8.0 in CUDA 11.0 / PTX ISA 7.0 and is fully available on A100; only TMA (cp.async.bulk.tensor) is new with Hopper sm_90. The finding is factually correct. Severity medium is arguably slightly generous (the error understates rather than overstates hardware capability, and the repo targets Blackwell anyway), but the paragraph teaches a general pattern and misleads Ampere readers, so medium/low boundary — leaving medium.

The checklist claims 'An NVL72 rack provides 130 TB/s total bisection bandwidth.' NVIDIA's 130 TB/s figure for GB200/GB300 NVL72 is the total aggregate bidirectional NVLink bandwidth (72 GPUs x 1.8 TB/s = 129.6 TB/s). The bisection bandwidth of the all-to-all NVSwitch fabric is roughly half that (~65 TB/s: 36 GPUs x 1.8 TB/s crossing the cut). Sizing collective-communication budgets against 130 TB/s of 'bisection' bandwidth overestimates the fabric by 2x. Line 129's garbled '(over 14" PCIe Gen5)' in the same section (a mangled 'over 14x PCIe Gen5') adds to the confusion.

EVIDENCE
An NVL72 rack provides 130 TB/s total bisection bandwidth.

SUGGESTED FIX

Change to 'An NVL72 rack provides 130 TB/s of aggregate bidirectional NVLink bandwidth (72 x 1.8 TB/s)' and, if a bisection figure is wanted, state ~65 TB/s; also repair line 129 to 'over 14x the bandwidth of a PCIe Gen5 x16 link'.

VERIFIER NOTES

Quoted sentence verified at docs/appendix.md:191 ('An NVL72 rack provides 130 TB/s total bisection bandwidth'). NVIDIA's 130 TB/s NVL72 figure is total aggregate bidirectional NVLink bandwidth (72 x 1.8 TB/s = 129.6 TB/s); bisection across the NVSwitch fabric is ~half (~65 TB/s, 36 GPUs' worth crossing the cut). Calling it bisection overstates the fabric 2x for collective sizing. The line 129 side-claim also verified: 'over 14" PCIe Gen5' is a mangled 'over 14x' (1.8 TB/s vs ~128 GB/s PCIe Gen5 x16). Confirmed at medium.

The profiling guide's commands fail as written. `ncu --metrics achieved_occupancy,warp_execution_efficiency` uses legacy nvprof metric names that Nsight Compute rejects ('Failed to find metric achieved_occupancy'); the modern equivalents are sm__warps_active.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_active and smsp__thread_inst_executed_per_inst_executed.ratio. The bandwidth figure printed at line 94 is (2*bytes)/iteration_time where the H2D and D2H cudaMemcpy calls run sequentially (synchronous memcpys, lines 80-86). PCIe 5.0 x16 provides ~64 GB/s per direction; 128 GB/s is the bidirectional aggregate that only applies when both directions transfer concurrently. Since the two copies never overlap here, this metric mathematically tops out near 64 GB/s (plus kernel time makes it lower), so presenting "~128 GB/s theoretical max" as the bottleneck for the printed number is a 2x-wrong hardware-spec comparison that will make readers think they achieve <50% of achievable link efficiency.

EVIDENCE
printf("Status: PCIe 5.0 bottleneck (~128 GB/s theoretical max)\n");

SUGGESTED FIX

State ~64 GB/s per direction as the ceiling for this sequential H2D+D2H metric (or overlap the copies on two streams with pinned buffers if the 128 GB/s aggregate figure is to be cited).

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: line 98 prints "~128 GB/s theoretical max" for the metric computed at line 94 as (2*bytes)/iteration-time, where the H2D copy (line 80), kernel (83), and D2H copy (86) run strictly sequentially with synchronous cudaMemcpy. PCIe 5.0 x16 is ~64 GB/s per direction; 128 GB/s is the bidirectional aggregate requiring concurrent transfers. This metric mathematically caps near 64 GB/s (lower still: pageable std::vector host memory and kernel time are included), so the 2x-wrong ceiling stands. Low severity is right for a misleading printed spec.

The buffer holds __nv_fp8_e4m3 values (lines 33/38/96). In E4M3 (bias 7), 1.0 is encoded as 0x38 (exponent 0111, mantissa 000); 0x3C has mantissa 100 and decodes to 1.5. (0x3C is 1.0 only in E5M2.) The teaching comment is factually wrong for the type in use; anyone extending the demo with a correctness check computed from "input = 1.0" would get failures, and repeated scaling by 1.5 starting at 1.5 saturates differently than claimed.

EVIDENCE
CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemset(d_input, 0x3C, bytes));  // Initialize to 1.0 in FP8

SUGGESTED FIX

Use 0x38 to initialize E4M3 values to 1.0 (or correct the comment to say 1.5).

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: line 105 `cudaMemset(d_input, 0x3C, bytes); // Initialize to 1.0 in FP8`, and the buffer is interpreted as __nv_fp8_e4m3 via fp8x8/fp8x32 (lines 32-39) and casts at 127/135. Decoded independently: E4M3 (bias 7) 0x3C = exp 0111, mantissa 100 = 1.5; 1.0 is 0x38; 0x3C is 1.0 only in E5M2. The comment is factually wrong for the type in use. No correctness check currently depends on it, so low is the right severity.

For the last tile, `elems = min(tile_span, count - offset)` and the copy size is `elems * sizeof(float)`. When count is not a multiple of 4 (e.g. count = 1'000'002 with tile_span 1024: last tile has elems = 578... any count % 4 != 0 tail), the byte count is not a multiple of 16, which violates the cuda::aligned_size_t contract ('behavior is undefined if size is not a multiple of the alignment'). The memcpy_async can then over-read/over-copy or misbehave depending on the libcu++ lowering, producing out-of-bounds global reads or corrupted shared data on the tail tile.

EVIDENCE
const size_t elems = min(tile_span, count - offset);
        cuda::memcpy_async(
            block,
            stage_ptr(stage),
            inputs + offset,
            cuda::aligned_size_t<16>(elems * sizeof(float)),
            pipe);

SUGGESTED FIX

Only use cuda::aligned_size_t<16> when (elems % 4) == 0 (full tiles); for the ragged tail, call cuda::memcpy_async with a plain size_t byte count, or round the copy region handling so the tail is copied element-wise.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified. Lines 45-51: elems = min(tile_span, count - offset); the last tile of the last block yields elems%4!=0 whenever count%4!=0 (tile offsets are always multiples of tile_span, which is 512*{4,6,8} — a multiple of 4). cuda::aligned_size_t<16>(elems*4) then violates the libcu++ contract, which requires the size to be a multiple of the alignment (UB — the lowering may issue 16B copies that over-read). Pointer alignment itself is fine (offsets are 16B-multiples off a cudaMalloc base). Reachability: the standalone demos use count = 1<<25 / 1<<26 (multiples of 4), so the bug is latent there, but threshold_kernels.cu takes count from an arbitrary tensor's numel(), so the torch-extension path can trigger it. Low severity is correct for a latent, edge-case contract violation.

The OPTIMIZATIONS list states '3. Larger cluster (8 CTAs) for more DSMEM benefit' and '4. No atomics needed - single writer per cluster', and the runtime output repeats 'No atomics (single writer per cluster)' (line 314). The code sets CLUSTER_SIZE = 4 (line 42), and STEP 2 has every CTA in the cluster perform `atomicAdd(leader_sum, block_sum)` through DSMEM (line 169) — four atomic writers per cluster, not one, and no 8-CTA cluster anywhere. In a book teaching cluster/DSMEM patterns, both statements misdescribe the actual synchronization mechanism the reader is supposed to learn from.

SUGGESTED FIX

Fix the comments and printf to describe the real scheme ('4-CTA cluster; each CTA's warp 0 atomically accumulates into the leader's shared memory via DSMEM'), or implement what is claimed: have each rank write to its own DSMEM slot and let rank 0 sum the four slots after cluster.sync(), removing the atomicAdd.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified. Header lines 10-11 claim 'Larger cluster (8 CTAs)' and 'No atomics needed - single writer per cluster'; the code sets CLUSTER_SIZE=4 (line 42) and every CTA's warp-0 lane-0 does atomicAdd(leader_sum, block_sum) through cluster.map_shared_rank DSMEM (lines 166-169) — four atomic writers per cluster. The runtime output repeats 'No atomics (single writer per cluster)' (line 313) directly after correctly printing '4-CTA cluster', and even the tuning comment at lines 43-50 admits a 'DSMEM atomic'. The synchronization itself is correct (init before cluster.sync, aggregate, sync, rank-0 writes), so this is purely misdescription — low is right.

console.print(f"[yellow]Generating flame graph from {file or 'default profile'}...[/yellow]")

SUGGESTED FIX

Either implement these against the existing backends (engine.profile.flame_graph()/memory_timeline()/kernels() already exist in core/engine.py) writing to the given --output path, or make the commands print an explicit "not implemented, use `aisp profile compare`" message and return a non-zero exit code, and remove the misleading "Generating..." text and --output option.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: aisp.py:817 registers 'flame' with help 'Generate flame graph' and an --output option defaulting to flame.html; profiling.py:414-420 (under the comment '# Placeholder implementations for other profile commands') only prints 'Generating flame graph from ...' plus a hint to use compare — no file read, no output written, returns None so exit code is 0. memory() (423-428) and kernels() (431-436) likewise print a header and do nothing, while aisp.py still accepts --output for memory. `elif current_gpu is not None and 'Link' in line and 'Active' in line.lower():` — `line.lower()` is all-lowercase, so `'Active' in line.lower()` is always False; the branch is unreachable (and its body is `pass` anyway), so discover_nvlink_topology() returns every GPU with an empty connection list. Downstream, `topo['nvlink_topology']` link listings (lines 438-440) are always empty and the interconnect classification at line 197 rests solely on whether any 'GPU N:' header line was parsed. The module currently has no importers, but as shipped example/analysis code its NVLink discovery is nonfunctional.

EVIDENCE
elif current_gpu is not None and 'Link' in line and 'Active' in line.lower():
                        # Has active NVLink
                        pass

SUGGESTED FIX

Compare in a consistent case (`'active' in line.lower()`) and actually record the link, e.g. append the link index/peer to `nvlink[current_gpu]` instead of `pass`, so the returned topology reflects active links.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified at line 125 (evidence comment at 126): `'Active' in line.lower()` is always False since line.lower() contains no uppercase characters — the branch is unreachable, and its body is `pass` anyway, so no link is ever recorded and every parsed GPU keeps the empty list assigned at line 122. Interconnect classification at 197 (`if nvlink_topo and len(local_gpus) > 1`) indeed rests only on whether a 'GPU N:' header parsed. Minor imprecision in the finding: the 438-440 topology section does print when headers parse — it just shows 'GPU N -> []' — but that doesn't rescue the code. Grep confirms no importers of the module. Low is right.

The transfer size is size_mb=1024 binary MiB (allocated as size_mb*1024*1024 bytes = 1 GiB = 1.0737e9 bytes), but the bandwidth formula treats size_mb/1024 as 1 decimal GB. The reported 'peak_bandwidth_gbs' is therefore 1.0737e9-byte transfers counted as 1e9 bytes: a link sustaining 900 GB/s reports ~838 GB/s. This measured value feeds the nvlink chapter targets, which are expressed in decimal GB/s, so the target comparison is systematically skewed.

EVIDENCE
size_mb = 1024\n        size = size_mb * 1024 * 1024 // 4  ... bandwidth_gbs = (size_mb / 1024) / (elapsed_ms / 1000) * iterations  (lines 675-676, 701)

SUGGESTED FIX

Compute from bytes with decimal units like the HBM path: bytes = size * 4; bandwidth_gbs = (bytes * iterations / (elapsed_ms / 1000)) / 1e9.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: size_mb=1024 with size = size_mb*1024*1024//4 elements (lines 675-676) makes each copy 2^30 bytes = 1.0737e9 bytes, but line 701 computes bandwidth as (size_mb/1024)=1 decimal 'GB' per transfer — reported GB/s is a factor 2^30/1e9 low (~6.9% under the true decimal value; equivalently the true value is ~7.4% above the reported one). One overstatement in the finding: NVLink chapter targets are static (performance_targets.py line 45: min 650 / target 725 GB/s) — build_targets_from_peak does not derive them from this measurement, so the skew is confined to the reported peak number itself. Low severity is right.

The gate refuses to run on anything below SM 10.0 and prints that TMA itself requires Blackwell. The Tensor Memory Accelerator (cp.async.bulk.tensor, cuTensorMapEncodeTiled) shipped with Hopper H100 (sm_90); Blackwell extends it (e.g. cta_group::2 loads on sm_100). In a book about GPU architecture this misstates which generation introduced the feature, and the check needlessly blocks Hopper machines from running a test that (as written) uses no TMA-specific instruction at all.

EVIDENCE
Lines 213-215: "if (prop.major < 10) {\n        printf(\"TMA requires Blackwell (SM 10.0+). This device is SM %d.%d\\n\", \n               prop.major, prop.minor);"

SUGGESTED FIX

Change the gate to prop.major < 9 and the message to 'TMA requires Hopper or newer (SM 9.0+)'; if the test is meant to exercise Blackwell-specific TMA behavior, implement actual cp.async.bulk.tensor loads and then gate on the Blackwell-specific feature being used.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: lines 213-216 gate on prop.major < 10 and print 'TMA requires Blackwell (SM 10.0+)'. The Tensor Memory Accelerator (cp.async.bulk.tensor, cuTensorMapEncodeTiled) shipped with Hopper H100 (sm_90) per NVIDIA's Hopper architecture documentation; Blackwell only extends it (e.g. cta_group::2). So the printed claim misstates the introducing generation and blocks Hopper needlessly. Severity lowered from medium to low: the gate guards a test that (per the confirmed 4096-thread-block finding) cannot pass on any hardware and uses no TMA instruction anyway, so the practical impact is a wrong message string; it remains worth fixing in a book about GPU architecture.

`re.findall(r"\\d+", line)` matches a literal backslash + 'd', which never occurs in version.h lines like `#define CUTLASS_VERSION_MAJOR 3`, so findall returns [] and `[0]` raises IndexError on the first MAJOR line. The `except (IndexError, OSError, ValueError)` at line 1427 converts this into the warning "Failed to parse CUTLASS version from ..." on every run, and `result["cutlass"]["version"]` stays None even when the checkout is present and valid — the dependency-health report is wrong whenever CUTLASS exists (same bug repeated at lines 1423 and 1425).

EVIDENCE
major = int(re.findall(r"\\d+", line)[0])

SUGGESTED FIX

Use `re.findall(r"\d+", line)` on all three lines (1421, 1423, 1425).

VERIFIER NOTES

od -c confirms line 1421 contains r"\\d+" (literal backslash-backslash-d), which matches only a literal backslash followed by 'd's — never present in '#define CUTLASS_VERSION_MAJOR 3'. findall returns [], [0] raises IndexError on the first MAJOR line, caught at 1427, warning appended, version stays None (line 1426 never runs). Same bug at 1423/1425. Downgraded to low: the failure is loudly surfaced via the 'Failed to parse' warning rather than silent, only the version string is lost, and path/sm100_headers fields still report correctly.

The script lives at code/core/scripts/, so one '..' resolves repo_root to code/core. Lines 38 and 43 then pushd "${repo_root}/ch07" and "${repo_root}/ch10" — but code/core/ch07 and code/core/ch10 do not exist (verified; the chapters live at code/ch07, code/ch10). pushd fails and set -euo aborts, so the documented TMA demo build helper can never build anything. Second layer: even with the correct root, 'make ARCH=sm_100 async_prefetch_tma' has no rule — ch07/ch10 only define suffixed targets (%$(TARGET_SUFFIX), e.g. async_prefetch_tma_sm100; ch10 defines tma_2d_pipeline_blackwell$(SUFFIX) at Makefile:141), and the echoed output paths (lines 49-50) are unsuffixed too.

EVIDENCE
Line 34: repo_root="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"  |  Line 38: pushd "${repo_root}/ch07" >/dev/null  |  Line 40: make ARCH="${ARCH}" async_prefetch_tma

SUGGESTED FIX

Use "/../.." like core/scripts/ci/run_compare_builds.sh does (repo_root -> code/), and build the suffixed targets (derive the suffix from ARCH, e.g. async_prefetch_tma_${ARCH#sm_} -> async_prefetch_tma_sm100) or invoke make with USE_ARCH_SUFFIX=0; fix the echoed binary paths to match.

VERIFIER NOTES

Both layers verified. Line 34's single '..' from code/core/scripts resolves repo_root to code/core; code/core/ch07 and code/core/ch10 do not exist (checked), so the pushd at line 38 fails and 'set -euo pipefail' (line 13) aborts. Second layer also real: ch07/Makefile:21 defines only the suffixed static pattern '$(TARGETS): %$(SUFFIX): %.cu' (USE_ARCH_SUFFIX defaults to 1 in cuda_arch.mk:112), so 'make ARCH=sm_100 async_prefetch_tma' has no rule, and the echoed unsuffixed binary paths at lines 49-50 are wrong too. Severity downgraded from medium to low: grep shows the script is referenced by no workflow, Makefile, doc, or other script, and it fails loudly at the first pushd rather than doing anything silently wrong — a broken, unused helper.

The fp8 scenario's code_example is `with torch.autocast(dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn):`. This fails on two counts: torch.autocast requires the positional `device_type` argument (TypeError as written), and float8_e4m3fn is not a supported autocast dtype (autocast supports float16/bfloat16/float32) so even `torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn)` raises. Anyone following this recommendation gets an immediate error; FP8 execution actually requires Transformer Engine's fp8_autocast or torch._scaled_mm, not torch.autocast.

EVIDENCE
"code_example": "with torch.autocast(dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn):\n    output = model(input)",

SUGGESTED FIX

Replace the example with a working FP8 pattern, e.g. `import transformer_engine.pytorch as te` + `with te.fp8_autocast(enabled=True): output = model(input)`, and adjust the requirements list to mention Transformer Engine.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: whatif.py:22 contains exactly the quoted code_example. Executed on torch 2.8.0: `with torch.autocast(dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn)` raises TypeError "autocast.__init__() missing 1 required positional argument: 'device_type'". And CUDA autocast only accepts float16/bfloat16 (float32 to disable) as the fast dtype, so even with device_type supplied the fp8 dtype is rejected on a CUDA machine; real FP8 execution goes through TE fp8_autocast or torch._scaled_mm. Low is right — it's a static advisory string, but the example is unrunnable as shipped.

In _stage_runtime_cache the current owner sends its active cache with dist.send(source, dst=target_rank) without .contiguous(). After the first chunk append, the active cache is the view returned by _extend_cache_buffer (line 128: 'return kv_buffer[:, :next_kv_len]') into a preallocated (batch, context_window, hidden) buffer. With the default batch_size=1 the size-1 leading dim keeps the slice contiguous, but for any CLI run with --batch-size > 1 the slice is non-contiguous (stride W*H over dim 0 vs. logical L*H), and NCCL point-to-point send on a non-contiguous CUDA tensor fails (ProcessGroupNCCL requires contiguous tensors), crashing the lab mid-iteration; the receiver meanwhile posts a matching recv into a contiguous (batch, current_cache_len, hidden) buffer (lines 374-379). Other sends in this file are guarded ('dist.send(chunk_kv.contiguous(), ...)' at line 565, 'dist.send(seed.contiguous(), ...)' at line 615), which shows the omission is unintentional.

EVIDENCE
dist.send(source, dst=target_rank)

SUGGESTED FIX

Send a contiguous copy: dist.send(source.contiguous(), dst=target_rank) — matching the .contiguous() calls already used for chunk_kv and seed sends in the same file — or keep a contiguous staging buffer per request for handoffs.

VERIFIER NOTES

The defect is real but the stated failure mode is version-dependent and wrong for current torch. Verified: line 367 sends `source` without .contiguous(); active_caches holds _extend_cache_buffer views 'kv_buffer[:, :next_kv_len]' (line 128) into a (batch, context_window, hidden) buffer (137-144), assigned at lines 573 and 1136 — contiguous only when batch_size==1 (default, line 43) or the slice fills the buffer; --batch-size is a real CLI flag (1371). The guarded sends at 565 (chunk_kv.contiguous()) and 615 (seed.contiguous()) confirm the omission is unintentional, and the receiver posts into a contiguous buffer (374-379). Correction: in torch 2.8, ProcessGroupNCCL::send calls check_gpu_single_tensor(tensor, p2p=true), which only TORCH_WARN_ONCE on non-contiguous P2P tensors (verified in v2.8.0 source, ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp lines 3228-3246 and 5265-5271) and then transmits data_ptr/numel — so batch_size>1 silently transmits interleaved junk rows into the peer's cache instead of crashing (older torch releases did throw 'Tensors must be contiguous'). Silent corruption on a non-default CLI path; low severity stands.

PROBLEM

The repo's pinned torch==2.9.1+cu130 wheels are manylinux_2_28 builds compiled with _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1; forcing =0 is the obsolete pre-2.6-wheel convention. Verified with a CMake repro that a linked target's INTERFACE compile options land AFTER target_compile_options on the command line: if TorchConfig propagates its ABI flag, torch's '=1' silently overrides this '=0' and the line is dead; if only the TORCH_CXX_FLAGS variable is exported (never referenced here), the module really compiles with ABI=0 and fails to link/import against libtorch with unresolved std::__cxx11::basic_string-ABI symbols. In no configuration is '=0' correct for the pinned stack.

EVIDENCE
Line 52: '-D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0' (repeated for CXX at line 55)

SUGGESTED FIX

Delete both -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0 occurrences; if an explicit flag is desired, derive it from the installed torch (append ${TORCH_CXX_FLAGS} from find_package(Torch), or query torch.compiled_with_cxx11_abi()).

VERIFIER NOTES

Lines 52 and 55 verified. The repo pins torch==2.9.1+cu130 (requirements_latest.txt:104), and the official pytorch.org cu130 wheels are manylinux_2_28 builds compiled with _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1 (PyTorch dropped the pre-cxx11 ABI wheels as of the 2.6-era manylinux_2_28 migration). Forcing =0 is therefore wrong for this stack in either scenario the reviewer describes: dead (torch's propagated =1 interface option wins as the later -D on the command line) or actively breaking (std::__cxx11 string symbol mismatches against libtorch). TorchConfig's TORCH_CXX_FLAGS is indeed never referenced in this CMakeLists. Low severity is right — it is masked or fatal-at-build, not a silent correctness bug.

PROBLEM

cyclic_multicast::cluster_id()/cluster_shape()/cluster_rank() are not defined anywhere in this repo or in CUTLASS/CuTe (repo-wide grep finds only these three uses), so any attempt to JIT this 'Stage 14: TMA Multicast' variant fails at compilation. Even if it compiled, the host builds tma_atom_B from TmaLoadA (plain SM90_TMA_LOAD, line 299 '// Use regular for now') and launches with a plain <<<>>> (line 314 comment: 'cluster launch needs cudaLaunchKernelEx which is complex'), so cluster_rank would always be 0 in the implicit 1x1x1 cluster and mcast_mask_b=0x3 would name a nonexistent CTA 1 — the kernel labeled multicast performs no multicast under any circumstances.

EVIDENCE
Lines 77-79: "dim3 cluster_id = cyclic_multicast::cluster_id();\n  dim3 cluster_shape = cyclic_multicast::cluster_shape();\n  uint32_t cluster_rank = cyclic_multicast::cluster_rank();"

SUGGESTED FIX

Replace with the real CuTe APIs (cute::block_id_in_cluster(), cute::cluster_shape(), cute::block_rank_in_cluster() from cute/arch/cluster_sm90.hpp), build tma_atom_B from SM90_TMA_LOAD_MULTICAST, and launch with cudaLaunchKernelExC + cudaLaunchAttributeClusterDimension as experimental/tcgen05_tma_multicast.cu already does — or delete the file in favor of that one.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: cyclic_multicast::cluster_id()/cluster_shape()/cluster_rank() at lines 77-79 are the only occurrences of that identifier in the entire repo, including the vendored code/third_party/cutlass tree — the namespace does not exist, so the TU cannot compile. Also verified the dead-multicast claim: the host builds tma_atom_B from TmaLoadA ('// Use regular for now') and launches with plain <<<>>> ('cluster launch needs cudaLaunchKernelEx which is complex'), so mcast_mask_b=0x3 would target a nonexistent CTA even if it compiled. Severity lowered from medium to low: no loader, Makefile, or Python path references this experimental file, so nothing ever attempts to build it — the defect is inert dead code misleading only readers who open it.

PROBLEM

The hardcoded gap-analysis text claims 'arithmetic intensity: 5461 FLOPs/byte'. For M=N=K=4096 with fp16 operands, AI = 2*M*N*K / (2 bytes * (M*K + N*K + M*N)) = M/3 = 1365 FLOPs/byte. 5461 (= 4*M/3) corresponds to forgetting that fp16 elements are 2 bytes and halving the traffic again. The compute-bound conclusion still holds (1365 >> 225), but the printed number is wrong and, being hardcoded, is also stale for any --size other than 4096.

EVIDENCE
Line 463: "  - We are COMPUTE BOUND (arithmetic intensity: 5461 FLOPs/byte >> 225 crossover)"

SUGGESTED FIX

Compute it from the actual run: ai = 2*M*N*K / (2*(M*K + N*K) + 4*M*N) (or 2-byte output if compared as fp16) and interpolate it into the f-string; for the default 4096 case print ~1365 FLOPs/byte.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: line 463 hardcodes 'arithmetic intensity: 5461 FLOPs/byte' inside the summary f-string. For M=N=K=4096 with 2-byte fp16 operands and output, AI = 2*M*N*K / (2*(MK+NK+MN)) = M/3 = 1365.3 FLOPs/byte (1024 if the fp32 output buffer is counted at 4 bytes); 5461 = 4M/3 corresponds to undercounting bytes by 4x. Default --size is 4096 (line 385) but the literal goes stale for any other size. The compute-bound conclusion survives either way (1365 >> 225). Low severity is correct — a wrong printed number in explanatory text, not executed logic.

PROBLEM

The baseline docstring says "Baseline for warp-specialized Triton decode ... keeps the Triton warp-specialized comparison workload-equivalent", and the pair is named *_decode_warp_specialized, but the optimized side (optimized_decode_warp_specialized.py, class CUDAGraphPersistentDecodeBenchmark) is a CUDA-graph replay of the standard eager PyTorch decode math — its own docstring admits "decode-only CUDA Graph replay with persistent prefill state". Any reader (or results table) attributing the measured speedup to warp specialization or a Triton kernel is being told something the code does not do; the delta measured is launch-overhead removal via CUDA graphs.

EVIDENCE
Lines 1-6: '"""Baseline for warp-specialized Triton decode: eager PyTorch math. ... This keeps the Triton warp-specialized comparison workload-equivalent."""' — while optimized_decode_warp_specialized.py line 1 reads '"""Optimized: decode-only CUDA Graph replay with persistent prefill state.' and contains no Triton kernel.

SUGGESTED FIX

Rename the pair (e.g. *_decode_graph_persistent) or rewrite both docstrings/labels to say the comparison is eager decode vs CUDA-graph-replayed decode; remove all "warp-specialized"/"Triton" wording, including the label strings passed to DecodeConfig.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified verbatim: baseline docstring lines 1-7 promise 'warp-specialized Triton decode' and a 'Triton warp-specialized comparison', while optimized_decode_warp_specialized.py line 1 says 'decode-only CUDA Graph replay with persistent prefill state' and its class (CUDAGraphPersistentDecodeBenchmark) contains only eager decode_fn calls captured into a CUDA graph; grep finds no Triton anywhere in the pair or decode_common.py. The measured delta is launch-overhead removal via graph replay, and the DecodeConfig labels (baseline line 68, optimized line 98) carry the misleading name into results tables. Low severity is correct: naming/documentation defect, no numerical error.

The module docstring (line 1) and class docstring (line 62 'MXFP8 KV-cache benchmark') describe the baseline as MXFP8 block scaling, but line 80-81 constructs `te_recipe.DelayedScaling(amax_history_len=16, amax_compute_algo="max")` — classic per-tensor delayed-scaling FP8, not MXFP8 (TE's block-scaled recipe is te_recipe.MXFP8BlockScaling). Readers comparing 'MXFP8 vs NVFP4 block scaling' are actually shown 'per-tensor FP8 vs NVFP4', which changes both the accuracy story (per-tensor scaling is far coarser than 32-element MX blocks) and the performance story of the lab's comparison.

EVIDENCE
"""Baseline KV-cache benchmark using MXFP8 block scaling."""

SUGGESTED FIX

Either switch the recipe to `te_recipe.MXFP8BlockScaling()` to match the docstrings, or correct the module/class docstrings (lines 1 and 62) to say 'FP8 delayed (per-tensor) scaling'.

VERIFIER NOTES

Line 1 docstring: 'Baseline KV-cache benchmark using MXFP8 block scaling'; line 62 class docstring: 'MXFP8 KV-cache benchmark'. Lines 80-81 construct te_recipe.DelayedScaling(amax_history_len=16, amax_compute_algo="max") — classic per-tensor delayed-scaling FP8. PROBLEM

expert_fc2 is declared as nn.Linear(hidden*2, hidden*num_experts), so its weight is [hidden*num_experts, hidden*2] with rows 0..hidden-1 belonging to expert 0. The forward slices 'self.expert_fc2.weight[:self.hidden_size, :]' for ALL selected experts, so the second projection is identical regardless of which experts the router picked — top-k routing only affects FC1. The adjacent comment calls this 'loses some efficiency', but it changes semantics, not efficiency: the class docstring ('Optimized sparse-routing MoE') describes per-expert computation that does not happen. The class is not used by OptimizedRouterTopKBenchmark (which uses GroupedTopKMoE), so it is dead-but-published teaching code that would silently produce non-expert-specific outputs if adopted.

EVIDENCE
fc2_out = torch.nn.functional.linear(selected_flat, self.expert_fc2.weight[:self.hidden_size, :])

SUGGESTED FIX

Gather each assignment's FC2 slice by expert id (e.g. view expert_fc2.weight as [num_experts, hidden, hidden*2], index with expert_ids, and use torch.bmm as GroupedTopKMoE does), or delete AdaptiveTopKMoE since the benchmark uses GroupedTopKMoE; at minimum correct the docstring/comment to state the FC2 is shared.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: expert_fc2 = nn.Linear(hidden*2, hidden*num_experts) (line 49) has weight [hidden*num_experts, hidden*2], and line 88 slices weight[:self.hidden_size, :] — expert 0's rows — for every selected expert, so routing only affects FC1; the adjacent comment ('loses some efficiency but compiles') mischaracterizes a semantic change as an efficiency tradeoff. OptimizedRouterTopKBenchmark instantiates GroupedTopKMoE (line 154), not AdaptiveTopKMoE; the only other consumers are hygiene tests (test_benchmark_hygiene_regressions.py ~8697-8724) checking differentiability, not FC2 semantics. Dead-but-published teaching code — low is the right severity.

test_cta_clustering runs forward passes with use_cta_clustering False/True and only prints output shapes, then prints '✅ CTA Clustering tests passed!' — there are zero assertions, so a clustering path that returns garbage logits or the wrong shape still passes. It also never checks the property that would validate the optimization (clustering on vs off producing equivalent outputs for identical weights — the two models are independently initialized, so it cannot). test_integration (line 199) is likewise assert-free. Under pytest these two collect and pass vacuously; under the __main__ runner only an exception can fail them.

EVIDENCE
print(f"✅ CTA clustering ON (below threshold): output shape = {logits_short.shape}")
print("✅ CTA Clustering tests passed!\n")   (lines 86-87; no assert anywhere in test_cta_clustering or test_integration)

SUGGESTED FIX

Build one model, run it with clustering toggled (or copy state_dict into both configs) and assert torch.allclose(logits_off, logits_on, ...) plus assert logits.shape == (2, 128, 1000); add the same shape/equivalence assertions to test_integration.

VERIFIER NOTES

Confirmed: test_cta_clustering (lines 18-87) contains zero asserts — only shape prints ending in '✅ CTA Clustering tests passed!' at 86-87 — and the OFF/ON models are independently init_weights()'d so no equivalence check is even possible as written. test_integration (199-250) is likewise assert-free. test_persistent_decode does have real asserts (139-193), which the reviewer correctly excluded. The __main__ runner catches Exception and prints '❌ TEST FAILED' without sys.exit, so even the script mode exits 0 on failure — slightly worse than claimed. Under pytest both assert-free tests pass vacuously.

sections:
PROBLEM

_get_packed_scales caches the to_blocked() results keyed by `_scale_cache_token`, which is (data_ptr, shape, strides, storage_offset, device, dtype, _version). `_version` only changes on in-place mutation of that tensor object; it is 0 for every freshly allocated tensor. When one input tuple is freed and generate_input() creates a new same-shape sfa/sfb (e.g. successive correctness tests of the same case shape with different seeds in an eval loop), PyTorch's caching allocator commonly returns the same device pointer, producing an identical cache key for different scale contents. _run_scaled_mm (used for the l==1,k==16384 case and as the universal fallback) then feeds the PREVIOUS input's blocked scales to torch._scaled_mm, yielding wrong outputs with no error.

SUGGESTED FIX

Key the cache on object identity while holding a reference that prevents pointer reuse — e.g. store the packed scales in a WeakKeyDictionary keyed by the sfa_ref/sfb_ref tensor objects (id() plus a kept strong/weak ref), or include a cheap content fingerprint (e.g. int hash of sfa_ref.view(torch.uint8)[:64].cpu() bytes) in the key.

VERIFIER NOTES

_scale_cache_token (lines 146-155) keys on data_ptr/shape/strides/offset/device/dtype/_version; nothing captures content identity. _version is identical (deterministically produced) for every freshly generated same-shape input, so the key collapses to the device pointer, and PyTorch's caching allocator commonly reuses a freed block for the next same-size allocation — a regenerated sfa/sfb at a reused address hits the previous input's cached to_blocked() scales. _run_scaled_mm (line 303) consumes them on the default l==1/k==16384 case0 path (custom_kernel line ~378) and the universal fallback (line 408); the 8-entry limit (line 29) clears on overflow but never invalidates on content change. Caveat tempering impact: in correctness testing a stale hit produces a visible mismatch failure rather than a silent pass; silent wrong outputs occur only in benchmark/timing loops (where inputs are typically reused as-is, the benign case). Real latent hazard, probabilistic trigger — low is fair.

PROBLEM

code/README.md:156 instructs users to run 'pip install -r requirements_latest.txt' in a fresh venv. The file pins 'torch==2.9.1+cu130' (line 104), but its only sources are PyPI (which publishes no +cu130 local-version wheels, so the '==2.9.1+cu130' specifier matches nothing) and '-f ./third_party/wheels' (empty on a fresh clone; setup.sh even deletes cached torch wheels), because the required index at line 18 is commented out. The documented quickstart therefore fails at torch resolution on any fresh checkout; CI only passes because benchmark-validation.yml line 133 adds '--extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130' out-of-band.

EVIDENCE
Line 18: '# --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130'  with line 104: 'torch==2.9.1+cu130' and README.md:156: 'pip install -r requirements_latest.txt'

SUGGESTED FIX

Uncomment the index as '--extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130' in requirements_latest.txt (extra-index keeps PyPI for everything else), or change the README command to include that flag as the CI workflow does.

VERIFIER NOTES

Core claim verified: requirements_latest.txt:18 has the index commented ('# --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130'), line 104 actively pins torch==2.9.1+cu130, README.md:156 tells users to 'pip install -r requirements_latest.txt' in a fresh venv, third_party/wheels does not exist on a fresh clone, and PyPI publishes no +cu130 local-version wheels (a local-version specifier requires an exact local match), so resolution fails. One citation error in the finding: the out-of-band '--extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130' lives in .github/workflows/tier1-nightly.yml:133-134, not benchmark-validation.yml:133 (benchmark-validation.yml installs CPU torch at line 91 and never installs the pinned wheel). That detail doesn't change the verdict: the documented quickstart is broken on a fresh checkout. Low severity is fair given setup.sh is the primary path (itself broken per finding 1).

The post-run checklist tells the operator cuDNN 9.15.1.9-1 is installed and 'matches PyTorch's compile-time version', but the install step at lines 1358-1376 explicitly installs and apt-mark holds libcudnn9-cuda-13=9.16.0.29-1 ('Installing cuDNN 9.16.0.29-1 for CUDA ...', with a fall-back to repo latest). An operator auditing the environment against the printed checklist records the wrong cuDNN version, and the 'matches PyTorch's compile-time version' rationale is unverifiable as stated.

EVIDENCE
Line 3897: 'echo "  • cuDNN: Installed 9.15.1.9-1 (matches PyTorch's compile-time version; PyTorch bundles 9.13.0 but we use system 9.15.1)"'  vs line 1362: 'echo "Installing cuDNN 9.16.0.29-1 for CUDA ${CUDA_SHORT_VERSION}..."'

SUGGESTED FIX

Update the summary line to report the actually-pinned 9.16.0.29-1 (ideally print the live 'dpkg -s libcudnn9-cuda-13' version instead of a hardcoded string) and correct or drop the bundled-version rationale.

VERIFIER NOTES

Verified: line 3897 prints 'cuDNN: Installed 9.15.1.9-1 (matches PyTorch's compile-time version...)' while the actual install block at lines 1359-1376 announces and installs libcudnn9-cuda-13=9.16.0.29-1 (with apt-mark hold, and a fall-back to repo latest that could be yet another version). The hardcoded summary is stale on every path and the 'matches PyTorch's compile-time version' rationale is unverifiable as printed. Cosmetic/audit-trail defect only; low is correct.

The module-level 'pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(not torch.cuda.is_available())' covers six tests, but five of them (test_ai_benchmarks_use_launch_bound_regime, test_tensor_core_streams_use_overlap_friendly_regime, test_allreduce_rmsnorm_uses_larger_fusion_workload, test_tpot_long_uses_transfer_heavy_config, test_vectorization_memory_uses_same_bandwidth_regime) only compare Python attributes and dataclass fields — no CUDA needed. Only the first test calls setup(). Result: a change that silently shrinks a benchmark workload regime (e.g. dropping vectorization N from 67M) passes every CPU environment, including any future CI pytest expansion, because the guard skips the whole file.

EVIDENCE
pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(not torch.cuda.is_available(), reason="CUDA required")   (line 19; e.g. line 84 'assert baseline.N == optimized.N == 67_108_864' is pure-CPU)

SUGGESTED FIX

Drop the module-level pytestmark and put @pytest.mark.skipif(not torch.cuda.is_available()) only on test_symmetric_memory_perf_uses_small_allocation_dominated_regime (the one that calls setup()/teardown() on device), so the five config-contract tests run on CPU-only hosts and CI.

VERIFIER NOTES

pytestmark skipif at line 19 confirmed, and the workload-regime assertions (e.g. line 84 'baseline.N == optimized.N == 67_108_864') are pure attribute checks, so the core claim holds. One correction to the reviewer's list of five CPU-safe tests: test_tensor_core_streams_use_overlap_friendly_regime is NOT CPU-safe — BaselineTensorCoresStreamsBenchmark.__init__ calls resolve_device(), which is partial(require_cuda_device, ...) per code/ch11/stream_overlap_base.py:15, so it raises without CUDA. The ch05/ch15/ch17/ch19 constructors are CPU-safe (verified: no device work in __init__). So 4 of the 6 tests could run on CPU, and the proposed fix must also keep the tensor-core test guarded. Severity low is right; note the file is not in CI anyway.

PROBLEM

test_kv_cache_demo_runs_on_gloo, test_multi_model_demo_runs_on_gloo, and test_speculative_demo_runs_on_gloo each begin with 'if not symmetric_memory_available() or torch.cuda.device_count() < 2: return'. On every CPU-only or single-GPU machine (including the CI runner, where the file isn't run anyway) the body never executes yet pytest reports the test as PASSED, not SKIPPED — so a broken demo is invisible and the suite's green count is inflated. The gate is also wrong for what the name promises: gloo is a CPU backend, so requiring >= 2 CUDA devices to exercise a gloo spawn guarantees the test never runs on exactly the hosts gloo exists for.

SUGGESTED FIX

Replace the silent 'return' with pytest.skip("requires symmetric memory and >=2 GPUs") so the state is visible, and if the workers genuinely run on gloo/CPU, drop the cuda.device_count() gate (or split into a CPU-gloo variant that actually runs in CI).

VERIFIER NOTES

The 'if not symmetric_memory_available() or torch.cuda.device_count() < 2: return' pattern exists exactly at lines 61-62, 73-74, 85-86, so the tests report PASS instead of SKIP on any host lacking prerequisites. The gate-vs-name criticism is real but in the opposite direction the reviewer framed: ch16.symmetric_memory_inference.init_distributed picks backend 'nccl' when CUDA is available (line 73), so with the required >=2 CUDA GPUs the spawned workers run NCCL — the '_on_gloo' path is literally never exercised. Requiring >=2 CUDA devices is however defensible since torch symmetric memory is a CUDA-only API. Severity downgraded to low: on capable hosts the demos do run and join; the defect is misleading reporting plus a misnomer, same class as the other silent-return findings the reviewer rated low.

PROBLEM

test_ch04_nvshmem_pairs_skip_cleanly_on_single_gpu_or_missing_symmem runs validate_pair for two nvshmem pairs but the only assertions are inside 'if torch.cuda.device_count() < 2:'. On the hosts that can actually run these pairs (>= 2 GPUs, e.g. the B200 box this book targets), the loop completes with zero assertions — a pair that hard-fails or reports valid=False passes the test silently. The sibling test at line 137 has the same shape but at least carries an else branch asserting result.valid; this one does not.

EVIDENCE
if torch.cuda.device_count() < 2:
    assert result.skipped is True
    assert result.error is not None and "SKIPPED" in result.error   (lines 448-450 — no else branch)

SUGGESTED FIX
